title: Blockade
developer: Gremlin Industries (designer Lane Hauck, programmer Ago Kiss)
publisher: Gremlin; Taito (JP, as Barricade II); Noval (Noval 760)
mechanics: two players each steer an arrow that leaves a permanent solid trail, so the free space shrinks as both players wall it off
crashing into either trail or the border scores a point for the opponent
the operator sets match length at 3-6 crashes
notes: Released November 1976 in North America and March 1977 in Japan. Hauck also built a four-player prototype, CoMotion, by November 1976. Japanese Wikipedia files this 'Tron game' under territory-taking games (陣取りゲーム).

title: Lock 'n' Chase
publisher: Data East; Taito (NA arcade); Mattel (Intellivision, Atari 2600)
mechanics: the player closes doorways behind them as temporary walls that trap the police
at most two doors closed at once; each reopens after a few seconds
some doors near the centre open and close on their own
money bags in the centre briefly stun the police, with escalating values (500 to 4000)
notes: Temporary walls that trap enemies, in a dot-collecting maze. Arcade release April 1981 in Japan and October 1981 in North America.

title: Make Trax
platforms: Windows (2021, Neo Geo Pocket Color Selection Vol. 1)
publisher: Kural Samno Electric (JP); Exidy (EU, as Crush Roller); Williams Electronics (NA, as Make Trax); SNK (NGPC)
mechanics: paint every path of the maze (a coverage goal with no enclosure)
two chasing fish enemies ('Ojaman'); touching one costs a life
two rollers on overpasses can be pushed along a corridor to crush enemies, which come back from an aquarium after a few seconds; crush points rise from 50 up to 9,000
enemies learn to dodge the rollers and try to trap the player
pop-in characters (cat, mouse, bird, tire, ghost cat, invisible man) leave footprints that must be painted again; catching one stops the tracks and scores
the NGPC remake redesigns the levels for the small screen
notes: Ninth highest-grossing arcade game of 1981 in Japan. Make Trax Turbo is a fan modification that speeds up the brush but not the fish. Korosuke Roller (コロスケローラー), with a squid player, warp passages and an emergency-warp button, is a separate follow-up and should be its own entry, not an alt title. The Gakken tabletop Paint Roller (1982) is entry 656.

title: Amidar
mechanics: movement is limited to the lines of a fixed Amidakuji (ladder) grid; the player cannot cut freely into the field
painting all four sides of a box fills it; the whole board must be filled
each filled box scores the value printed inside it
stages alternate: odd stages are dot/coconut collecting (ape), even stages are edge painting (paint roller)
roller stages: new boxes must touch already-claimed territory, and the roller runs out of paint if it strays too far from filled boxes, at which point unfinished lines vanish
filling the four corner boxes briefly makes enemies killable (200/400/800/1,600 points)
jump button (3 uses per level or life) makes all enemies jump so the player can pass under them
deterministic 'Amidar movement': enemies travel vertically and take every available horizontal turn
a white Tracer patrols the perimeter counterclockwise, then follows the player's exact path after a set number of laps (sooner on later stages)
later levels add more and faster enemies and more complex grids
Amidakuji bonus stage between levels (5,000-point prize)
notes: Considered the first grid-capture (line-colouring) game. The arcade game launched in Japan in March/April 1982 per both Wikipedias; KLOV gives 1981 and has a 1981 German flyer. Stern distributed a harder ROM set and Konami an easier one. Many unlicensed bootlegs circulated as 'AMIGO'. Clones include Time Runner, Kid Grid, Jeepers Creepers, Omidar, Rollo and the Brush Bros. and Spiderdroid.

title: Disco No. 1
mechanics: instead of claiming area, the roller-skater scores by skating a complete loop around one or more tough guys
encircling several tough guys in one loop is the core scoring play
bonus items drift across the rink to collect
1-2 players, alternating
notes: Thin Ice (Intellivision, sold by INTV in 1986; developed during Mattel's ownership) is a separate game that Wikipedia calls a clone of Disco No. 1 and deserves its own entry. Its mechanics are not Disco No. 1's: a penguin leaves a white trail on the ice, carving out sections sinks them, the goal is to sink five penguins, a red seal chases you, a polar bear can be frozen with a side button, and a Zamboni plays between levels. The Sweet Heart variant is a DECO Cassette US release in MAME.

title: Hot Shocker
mechanics: the player (Dudley) recolours the strands of a web by walking along them
skeletons chase the player across the web
notes: Web-painting maze game in the Amidar family, not a Qix area-capture game. MAME catver: Maze / Outline (hotshock, hotshockb). The early revision shows 'Dudley presents' where the later one names Domino. Wikipedia's arcade list spells the maker 'E.G. Felago'. Controls: 8-way joystick and one button, single player with alternating play for 2.

title: Pepper II
mechanics: each level is four connected mazes that must all be filled; the playfield spans four screens
the player leaves a zipper trail and enclosing a segment fills it; going back over an unfinished segment unzips it
the Whippersnapper (Zipper Ripper on ColecoVision) unzips any unfinished segment it crosses
enclosing a corner pitchfork turns the player into a devil for about 4 s: Roaming Eyes can be eaten and the Whippersnapper freezes
a centre energizer alternates between pitchfork and halo; enclosing it on the halo removes the Whippersnapper from the maze
each maze hides a prize under one segment, awarded when that area is enclosed
extra turn at a DIP-switch threshold (40k/50k/70k/90k points)
notes: Grid-capture game across four screens, designed and programmed by Larry Hutcherson. The ColecoVision port supports 1-2 players and four skill levels. There was no 'Pepper I'.

title: Quantum
mechanics: the trackball probe leaves a tail; crossing it to close a loop destroys the particles inside
the stage clears when all nuclei are destroyed
touching particles or active red bonds destroys the probe; only electrons are safe to touch
notes: Released November 1982. A remake, Quantum: Recharged, came out in 2023 for Switch, PS4/PS5, Windows and Xbox.

title: Triple Punch
mechanics: playfield is a grid wider than the screen that scrolls horizontally and wraps around
fill rectangles by colouring every line around them, as in Amidar
completing two rectangles at once doubles the points and three at once quadruples them
an eraser enemy removes lines you have already painted
three quick punches knock out the eraser, ghost or gorilla, and an ambulance carries it off
a fire enemy cannot be punched and is always deadly
notes: The player is a carpenter who looks like Mario. MAME sets triplep and knockout, catver category Maze / Outline. Sold as a conversion kit and as an upright cabinet.

title: Libble Rabble
mechanics: twin-stick control of two arrows joined by a line that wraps around poles to form loops
enclosing Mushlins harvests them; loops you close yourself score more; a season ends when all are harvested
looping enemies: most are sent to the top of the screen for a short time; Killers, Changers and Demons are destroyed
Shears and Demons cut the line, which then reforms between the arrows
a detector signals when a closed area holds a hidden chest; you open it by enclosing a small area that covers only the chest and no other possible hiding place
Topcups released from chests must be corralled and looped to earn bonus letters; a completed word opens a timed bonus stage
the border is a timer; looping Mushlins and plants adds time

title: Rollo and the Brush Brothers
mechanics: Amidar remake: Rollo, a paint roller, paints the maze lines to box in grid squares while the enemy paint brushes (the Brush Brothers) chase him
notes: Wikipedia's Windmill Software navbox lists it under 1983, but the Amidar article says Windmill published it in 1984 as a self-booting IBM PC disk. Dosgames lists a 1995 freeware release. CGA graphics, PC speaker sound. Dosgames describes it as 'kinda like Pac-Man meets Qix'.

title: Zoo Keeper
developer: Taito America (designers Keith Egging, John Morgan)
mechanics: zoo stage: the player runs along the edges of a rectangle, laying a brick wall behind him
animals bounce around inside and break holes in the wall where they hit it
escaped animals run along the outer edge toward the player, who must jump over them; jumping several at once scores exponentially more
a net power-up briefly lets the player herd animals back into the central cage
when the stage timer runs out, each animal still inside the wall scores points
notes: Sold as a conversion kit for Taito's Qix cabinets. A perimeter-defence relative of Qix: repairing a breakable border against bouncing enemies, plus edge-running chasers, is relevant to minions that patrol the edges. The game cycles through the zoo stage, a platform stage and an escalator bonus stage; only the zoo stage is territory-related.

title: Gridd Worz
publisher: Your Computer (IPC Electrical-Electronic Press), vol. 4 issue 7, July 1984 type-in
mechanics: there is no enclosure: you clear a 26x20 grid one cell at a time by flying over it, and the level ends once about 75% of the cells are gone
the ship keeps moving in its last direction, like a Tron light-cycle, and the keys only steer it
Drones (one per level, up to four) bounce around the grid and lay cleared cells back down as they pass, undoing your progress
re-crossing cells you have already cleared, or bumping the edge, adds cells back to the remaining count and makes the Drones home in on you
each level adds one more lethal fixed obstacle in a random cell; 3 lives
notes: The magazine's in-game story calls it 'destroying the individual Gridd sections' until about 75% is gone, after which 'the network explodes'. It is a cell-clearing painter with Tron-style steering rather than a Qix area-capture game. The mechanics come from the BASIC and assembly listing on the archived disc.

title: Itazura Tenshi
mechanics: the angel connects constellations by flying into scattered stars, so lines run between fixed points rather than enclosing area
the angel shoots arrows to fend off enemies
a completed constellation scores a bonus that grows with its size; each stage has a set number of constellations
after the constellations of a stage, a bonus event reunites Ran and Lum (in the manner of Altair and Vega) for extra points
notes: Japan-only arcade release in November 1984; Hamster released it outside Japan for the first time on 4 November 2022. Wikipedia calls it a multidirectional shooter. Its link to territory capture is only the star-connecting; it claims no area.

title: Rumba Lumber
platforms: Taito Egret II mini Arcade Memories Vol. 3 (2024)
mechanics: the player hacks down trees (about two hacks each); each felled tree shrinks the enemy's space and opens ground for the player, as in Dig Dug
goal: trap the pterodactyl, which can fly only over trees, in a clump of four or fewer trees
the scene score multiplies the trees left uncut by a bonus that grows as the trap gets smaller, so efficient captures pay more
the pterodactyl bounces diagonally, wraps around screen edges through tree rows, and starts breathing fire as the scene goes on
a limited number of stone wheels per scene (second button plus a direction) kill the dinosaur and mole; hitting the pterodactyl ends the scene at once
a dinosaur hatched from an egg walks through trees, and a mole surfaces and tracks the player briefly
four scenes loop with their own hazards: a river (scene 2), a cloud that regrows cut mushrooms (scene 3), a fireball volcano (scene 4); later loops add uncuttable dead trees
notes: Taito Japan's Qix/Dig Dug hybrid about trapping the enemy by reshaping terrain, with no safe edge to retreat to. The title screen and the MAME driver say 1984; the Japanese reference book アーケードTVゲームリスト (ISBN 978-4990251215), not MAME, gives a September 1985 release. Its MCU protection was only defeated in 2017.

title: Clax
mechanics: the field is a grid of coloured blocks; moving across the borders between blocks swaps their colours, which is how territory is taken
three enemy smileys are trapped when their colour matches the block they stand on; a trapped smiley stops moving
a trapped smiley's last position stays lethal but becomes invisible, so the player must remember it
trapping two smileys at once scores far more than one; clearing a level adds a time bonus
levels are timed: surviving until the timer ends advances without capture points or time bonus
colours are random per level; after level 10 the blocks get smaller and more numerous; touching a smiley ends the game
notes: Soviet DOS game, filed by old-games.ru as Xonix-like; the reviewer says it has its own mechanics, and its author made several other Xonix-themed games.

title: Dig Dug II
alt_titles: Dig Dug II: Trouble in Paradise
mechanics: a jackhammer cracks the island along predefined fault lines
when cracks split the island, the smaller part sinks, killing everything on it, the player included if careless
score scales with the number of enemies sunk at once
a bonus vegetable appears after three pieces are cut off
an air pump inflates enemies; Fygars also breathe fire
the last 1-3 enemies flee to the edge and jump into the sea, ending the round
notes: Territory cutting with a 'smaller piece sinks' rule instead of a boss-free-region rule. Arcade release March 1985 in Japan; Arcade Archives April 2023.

title: Spider Web
mechanics: spider moves inside a bordered rectangular field and spins straight web strands (one button starts and stops a strand)
strands persist and build up a web that catches flies; clear the level by catching all flies before they overpopulate
the more strands on the field, the fewer flies may be active at once (wall-building progressively constrains enemies)
spider can kill flies directly while suspended on a strand, or zap them with Space/right mouse button
mouse or 8-direction keyboard control (number-pad diagonals)
notes: EGA shareware ('I trust you' donation basis). The author's SPIDER.DOC on archive.org describes the rules above, and the archive.org screenshot shows the spider hanging on a strand from the top border of a framed field with a 'Flys left' counter. It is a line/wall-building game rather than strict area capture, hence adjacent-genre. It is unconfirmed that this is the 'Spider Web' the Qixote wiki lists, because the wiki gives no details. archive.org also has a C64 'Spider Web' (Alpha Software, (c) 1983 A.V.L.), whose gameplay I could not check.

title: Mr. Do! Run Run (Atari ST)
developer: Martin Bysh (code), Gary Felix (graphics), Wally Beben (music); game design by Universal
mechanics: Mr. Do leaves a rope line behind him as he runs; looping the rope around dots ('inscribing') turns them into cherries
inscribing fruit again upgrades it a tier (cherry, apple, lemon, pineapple), worth more points and more powerball recharge
inscribing can turn a fruit into a flashing EXTRA letter; running over it releases an Alpha-Monster with three henchmen, and defeating it locks in the letter
a screen clears when all dots and fruit are eaten or all regular monsters are defeated
logs can be rolled downslope to crush monsters, and a bouncing powerball scores more with each bounce
notes: Licensed Atari ST port of Universal's 1984 arcade game Do! Run Run, the fourth Mr. Do! game; Wikipedia also lists Amiga and MSX versions. Atarimania tags the ST port 'Arcade - Qix'. The mechanics come from Wikipedia's description of the arcade original; how closely the ST port follows them is not verified.

title: Rampart
mechanics: timed build phase: place Tetris-like wall pieces to close gaps and fully enclose castles; pieces are often larger than the gaps, so leftover pieces make later repairs harder
each fully enclosed castle grants cannons (the home castle grants two), which are placed only inside your enclosed territory
after combat, any area no longer fully walled in is lost along with the cannons inside it
you lose if no castle is enclosed when a build phase ends
battle phase: ships (single player) or the rival player (versus) shoot your walls; you fire slow cannonballs that must lead moving targets
enclosing bonus squares awards extra points
2-player versus, with each side's territory separated by rivers
notes: Enclosure as territory, with a build, battle and repair cycle. Played with a trackball. North American arcade release October 1990. A 2007 PlayStation Network version added online multiplayer.

title: Splash!
developer: OMK Software (Barcelona freelance group; Gaelco did music and sound)
mechanics: a brush moves freely in 8 directions and erases the blue overlay wherever it passes, revealing a picture of a woman (painting, not line capture)
an on-screen completion percentage and a timer; some levels do not require full coverage
bubbles bounce around the screen, and touching one costs a life (3 lives)
limited, non-refillable ammo of 50 shots to pop bubbles; popped bubbles eventually reappear
popped bubbles leave red stars that turn into bonus coins when touched
bombs can be dropped anywhere; they stay put and explode when a bubble touches them
66 stages
2-player simultaneous play
notes: Spanish image-reveal painting game. MAME files it as Puzzle / Paint and credits it to 'Gaelco / OMK Software'. Microhard's The Return of Lady Frog is a hack or bootleg of its hardware.

title: Achtung, die Kurve!
alt_titles: Curve Fever (name of the later remake series)
developer: Filip Oščádal (Fred Brooker) and Kamil Doležal
mechanics: 2 to 8 players (up to 6 in the original) on one screen
each dot moves at constant speed and leaves a permanent solid trail
two buttons steer left and right with a limited turn rate, giving curved, non-cardinal trails
hitting any trail or the border eliminates you; trails stay until the game ends
random gaps open in trails, letting a player escape an enclosure
last surviving player wins the round
notes: Freeware clone of the 1993 Czech game Červi; its main addition is the gaps in trails. Not a capture game, but a known reference for curved lethal trails and escape gaps in versus play. Remakes include Zatacka, Curve Fever (2011), Curve Fever Pro and Curve Crash.

title: Lady Killer
mechanics: the chosen woman's picture is shown briefly, then covered by a board of tiles
the diver dives into the board and surfaces to flip tiles; flipping every tile clears the level
flipped tiles often hold power-ups
touching or being shot by an enemy kills you; flipping the tile an enemy stands on kills it; enemies respawn until the level ends
the woman's silhouette stays visible on the board
eight women, four stages each, with the picture changing between stages
each woman has a special stage: a sliding-tile puzzle or a number-selection game
continuing restarts the current level
notes: Released December 1993. Wikipedia lists it among Gals Panic clones, and MAME files it as Puzzle / Outline, but the core is tile flipping, not line capture. The export set has a 'Nudity' DIP switch that Moeyo Gonta!! lacks. Sequel: Party Time: Gonta the Diver II (1995).

title: Painter
publisher: ST Format / Future Publishing (shareware, later public domain)
mechanics: walk a grid of lines; each line you pass changes colour, and colouring every side of a rectangle fills it
some lines are hidden and only flash at level start, so the grid must be memorised
enemies always take the most direct route to you and can see hidden lines, so their paths reveal them
fire drops a hole in the grid that blocks pursuers but stops you doubling back
100 levels with passwords; registered users get a level designer
notes: Atarimania calls it a Qix-style game, but it plays as an Amidar-style line painter. The Atari Jaguar conversion is listed only in Atarimania's trivia and was not checked further. The Qixote fan wiki lists it by name under 'Sundry'.

title: The Return of Lady Frog
mechanics: drop bombs that each clear a 3x3 area of the grid covering a photo; the stage is cleared by uncovering the picture
bombs also break grey square barriers that block paths
bombs do not hurt balloons, but a balloon rolling over a bomb as it explodes smothers the blast and leaves that area covered
fire bottle-rockets at balloons; a popped balloon drops point items or splits into smaller balloons
skull-and-crossbones balloons cannot be destroyed and must be avoided
being hit by a balloon costs a life
2-player play
notes: Italian hack or bootleg of Gaelco's Splash! board. It is not a sequel to the 1990 Frogger clone Lady Frog. MAME files it as Shooter / Outline.

title: Harapeko Bakka
mechanics: dinosaurs walk on a 9x9 grid and automatically drop eggs of their colour along their path to claim squares
surrounding an opponent's eggs converts them to your colour (Othello-style enclosure capture), allowing late reversals
a player can eat laid eggs (B button) to change their colour; this costs time and can leave them outmanoeuvred
the player with the most eggs wins
up to 4 simultaneous players with a multitap
single-player mode of 50 stages of rising difficulty
notes: A competitive enclosure-capture party game rather than a Qix clone: the trail is a line of eggs that captures by surrounding. Never released in North America. Reviews were mixed to poor.

title: Party Time: Gonta the Diver II
mechanics: adult-themed tile-flipping picture reveal, following Lady Killer's diver
notes: Sequel to Lady Killer (Moeyo Gonta!!), released May 1995. MAME files it as Puzzle / Outline. 2 players, 8-way joystick, 3 buttons.

title: Penky
mechanics: timed rounds of 40-70 seconds (30-60 s on the Italian set), set by DIP switch
a round is won by covering a minimum share of the surface (70-99.9% by DIP) or by holding the majority when time runs out
versus play over 1 bout or best of 3 (2 or 3 matches)
optional strip-tease pictures as the reward
notes: MAME catver: Maze / Change Surface (penky, penkyi). 1-2 players at once, 8-way joystick, one button. Board YS951004. The Italian Impeuropex set adds a Redemption mode that pays out tickets for points. The rules come from DIP switch lists quoted in the MAME driver; no gameplay description was found, so how a player claims surface is unverified.

title: firmament i-a
publisher: flatearth software (self-published; shareware at release, now listed as freeware)
mechanics: clusters of small diamond-shaped pieces flow down from the top in varied formations; the line drawn by moving the mouse pointer encloses them, and enclosed pieces vanish while the rest keep flowing
missed pieces cross a dead-end line and stack at the bottom; a stack 4 or more rows high ends the game
score = basic points x efficiency x speed x sequence, shown as a formula for every erasure
basic points rise the lower on the field the pieces are erased
efficiency multiplier = piece area divided by enclosed area, rewarding tight enclosures
speed multiplier from the player-chosen maximum flow speed (4 steps); pieces accelerate as they flow
sequence multiplier (up to 9.99x) for erasing the next piece while the previous erasing line is still on screen
modes: normal, extreme, and score attack (no stack game over, a penalty per missed piece, 10-minute limit)
notes: Lasso-enclosure action puzzle with a monochrome look. The author split one concept in two: the action-puzzle half became firmament i-a, and a Game-of-Life-style 'god's-eye view' half became firmament i-b. The 2002 date in the original entry matches a later build (20021010), not the first release.

title: Brainstorm (TI-86)
mechanics: you have only three lines to capture a ball inside the point-giving areas
notes: Known only from the one-line ticalc.org archive description of brainst.zip (v1.0, 13 KB). The listing date 02-02-16 is read as 16 February 2002, since the listing uses YY-MM-DD (it dates Jezzball 86 as 99-05-03). The capture rule resembles JezzBall's wall-building, but no more detail was found.

title: Star Trigon
developer: Namco (Project Driller); ports by Namco Networks
mechanics: the player hops from planet to planet, and the jumps form large triangles
creatures (Uchijins) inside a completed triangle are rescued (enclosure capture); the stage ends when all are rescued
the player automatically circles the planet they stand on and must time each jump, or they fall off and lose a life
an oxygen meter drains during the stage and is refilled with air capsules
selectable characters differ in speed and oxygen use
later stages speed up and add hazards: large flares and black holes that pull the player in
notes: Enclosure capture through triangles formed by jumps instead of drawn trails. GAME Watch compared its controls to Libble Rabble and Katamari Damacy.

title: Dig Dug: Digging Strike
mechanics: dig underground on the bottom screen and line up large stakes to create fault lines
a completed fault line breaks off a section of the island on the top screen and sinks it, which is how the boss is sunk
two-screen play: island and boss on the top screen; player, enemies and stakes on the bottom
enemies are defeated by pumping them up or pushing them into rocks, lava or quicksand
enemies can carry food to the boss to make it stronger
items: magnets, time-stopping clocks, boxing gloves
some power-ups summon Susumu (after a minigame) to drive a stake in with a dropped weight or to stun the boss
collecting all fossils unlocks a bonus stage
notes: Fifteen stages. Combines Dig Dug's digging with Dig Dug II's island-sinking fault lines.

title: Yoshi Touch & Go
mechanics: draw a circle around an enemy to trap it in a bubble (lasso capture)
draw lines that become cloud paths carrying the character around hazards and opening alternate routes
blow into the microphone to erase drawn clouds
versus: clearing enemies sends spiky obstacles to the opponent's screen
modes: Score Attack, Marathon, unlockable Time Attack and Challenge
notes: Enclosure is a lasso around single enemies, not area capture.

title: Pokémon Ranger
mechanics: capture by drawing consecutive loops around a moving Pokémon with the stylus
each Pokémon needs N loops; a counter above it drops by one per completed loop
the combined loop length is capped; the cap grows with Styler level, so tight loops near the target are riskier and bigger loops need upgrades
if the Pokémon touches the capture line it breaks and the loops reset (Qix-style)
Pokémon attacks damage the Styler's HP; plain collisions mostly do not; at 0 HP you restart from the last save
Poké Assist: captured Pokémon can be spent to help with harder captures; the partner Plusle or Minun can paralyze the target, and successful loops recharge its energy
captured Pokémon are used once for a field move or assist, then released
notes: A free-form, stylus take on Qix's 'enemy touches your open line' rule. Japan release March 2006.

title: Dig Dug Island
alt_titles: Dig Dug Island: Minami no Shima no Pukupukupon
ディグダグアイランド〜南の島のプクプクポン〜
publisher: VerX Inc. (Bellx / ベルクス, distributed via Vector)
mechanics: Dig Dug II island-cutting moved online: drill cracks along fault lines, and when they split the island the smaller piece sinks with every enemy on it
free-to-play online multiplayer action instead of single-player arcade
notes: Japan-only online game. Closed beta December 2007, service launched 8 May 2008, ended 21 April 2009. Wikipedia calls it an online version of Dig Dug II. The online rules (player count, teams) were not found, so the island-cutting mechanic is inferred from Dig Dug II.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ディグダグアイランド

title: Pokémon Ranger: Shadows of Almia
platforms: Wii U Virtual Console (Europe and North America, 2016)
mechanics: a Friendship Gauge filled by loops replaces the fixed count of unbroken loops
lift the stylus to dodge attacks without losing progress, but the gauge drains if you stop looping too long
levelling the Styler makes each loop fill more of the gauge
the Fine Styler can be held to charge for quicker captures, and the charge can be upgraded
partner Pokémon is chosen, not set by gender: 17 possible partners, one per type
notes: Japan release 20 March 2008. Followed by Pokémon Ranger: Guardian Signs (2010), which is a separate entry.

title: Pokémon Ranger: Guardian Signs
mechanics: capture by drawing loops around a Pokémon with the Capture Styler
a Pokémon that breaks the loop by attacking drains styler energy; at zero energy the styler breaks and the game reverts to the last save
a Pokémon crossing the line without attacking breaks the loop at no energy cost
experience from captures and missions unlocks styler upgrades (power, energy capacity); later the styler can be charged for stronger captures
partner Pokémon can be called in to help a capture
drawn 'Ranger Signs' summon Legendary Pokémon for use outside battle
up to 4-player co-op missions
notes: Third Pokémon Ranger game. Japan release 6 March 2010.

title: Game Maker Qix
mechanics: antivirus theme: the playfield border is a ring of folder icons; the marker travels along it and touches infected (red) files to clean them (they turn cyan)
marker can leave the border and draw a dotted Stix trail, chased along the trail by a Qix-style Fuse (seen in the screenshot)
Spritz enemies are removed by touching them; Sparx patrol the border and the Qix roams the field, and both must be avoided
HUD tracks score, cleaned-file count and an Energy meter
final phase: once all files are clean, shoot the cleaned files at the Qix to destroy it
notes: The author says it is 'heavily based on Qix and slightly based on the game maker tutorial game and Jaws for the NES'. The itch.io screenshot shows Qix's full layout. The red marker is drawing a dotted trail into the field with a fuse burning along it, orange Sparx are on the border, the green Qix and blue star-shaped Spritz are in the field, and the HUD reads 'Cleaned files: 4'. No filled or claimed area is visible, so it is unconfirmed whether closing a trail captures territory. The core is edge-walking and trail-drawing, but the win condition is touching the files and then a shooting boss phase, hence adjacent-genre. itch.io tags are Arcade, atari, qix and Retro, and the download is Game_maker_qix_v9_2011.exe (5.3 MB).

title: Hundreds
platforms: Flash (2010 prototype, never sold; source later released)
developer: Semi Secret Software with Greg Wohlwend
mechanics: no line drawing: touching a circle grows it and counts its number up; the level clears when the numbers total 100
a circle that touches another circle while it is being grown fails the level
100 handcrafted levels add linked circles that must be touched together, buzzsaws that reset numbers, and snowflakes that freeze other circles
hidden cipher puzzles appear between levels; an endless mode of random levels unlocks after level 100
notes: Released on iOS on 7 January 2013 and on Android on 28 June 2013. Game Developer (Gamasutra) called it the inverse of JezzBall: you fill space with growing bodies among moving ones, with a fixed numeric goal. The 2010 Flash original by Wohlwend was simpler and was open-sourced after Flash portals passed on it.

title: Ingress
developer: Niantic (Niantic Labs at Google; Niantic Inc.; Niantic Spatial from 2025)
mechanics: location-based: two factions capture and link real-world portals
linking three portals in a triangle creates a control field that claims the Mind Units beneath it
Mind Units scale with the human population under the field, so bigger enclosures score more
an enemy breaks a field by destroying any one of its links; a portal left with fewer than 3 resonators loses all its links and fields
notes: Team territory capture by triangular enclosure rather than with a trail. Closed beta November 2012, Android release 14 December 2013, iOS 14 July 2014; relaunched as Ingress Prime on 5 November 2018. Listed among pages linking to 陣取りゲーム (territory games) on Japanese Wikipedia.

title: Spider: Rite of the Shrouded Moon
mechanics: the spider jumps between surfaces trailing silk; strands that close a triangle form a web that catches flying insects (series rule documented for the predecessor Spider: The Secret of Bryce Manor)
a jump across too wide a gap breaks the strand (documented for the predecessor)
silk is limited: trap insects before you run out
each level has an insect quota that opens the exit portal; you may stay to keep eating
hornets cannot be webbed and must be attacked by jumping into them
real-world time of day, weather and location change insect placement and puzzles; 30 levels
notes: Sequel to Spider: The Secret of Bryce Manor (iOS, 2009). Released 6 August 2015 on mobile and PC, and 25 October 2016 on PS4 and Vita. The Qixote wiki lists it under 'Closish Enough' as 'an interesting adaption on the Qix model'. Its own sources do not spell out the strand geometry, so the enclosure details come from the predecessor.

title: Splatoon (Turf War)
mechanics: online 4v4 teams ink the map; the team covering the most turf in its colour after 3 minutes wins
in squid form you swim through your own team's ink (including up walls) to move fast, hide and refill ink
enemy ink slows you in humanoid form, cannot be swum through and slowly damages you
splatted players respawn at their team's starting point
notes: Territory by surface coverage, not by enclosure. Released 28-30 May 2015.

title: Ink Dots: Territory Capture
mechanics: two ink colours of dots on one grid; surrounding rival dots with an unbroken chain captures them
goal is to claim the most territory; play against a friend or the AI
notes: A pocket Go-like, in the tradition of the pen-and-paper Dots game. Version 1.0 released 6 July 2026; free with optional tips and no ads.

title: Lazy Drawer: Line Survivors
mechanics: no weapons or aiming: your walking trail is the attack, and enemies touching it take damage over time
closing a loop bursts damage on everything inside; bigger loops trap more enemies
dash out of danger while managing a trail gauge
pick 1 of 3 upgrades per level from 30+; maxed upgrades awaken; 26 hidden synergies tracked in a codex
10 stages, each with its own waves, a mid-boss and a boss; ~15-minute runs; toggleable per-stage Overtime Conditions
5 characters; 18 collectible charms bought with run gold, with set bonuses that shape the starting build
notes: Survivors-like built on loop enclosure. Released 5 November 2026; demo available.

title: Linsips
mechanics: exactly one horizontal and one vertical line split the field into four quadrants
a goal of equal ball counts in every quadrant replaces a percentage target
each ball has its own speed, trajectory and size
the first line cannot be undone, and the clock and balls keep moving while you place the second
20 levels, from four-ball setups to multi-ball ones
notes: Free on Steam, released 17 March 2026, with an MS-DOS look and an OPL3 FM soundtrack. A puzzle with a set objective instead of a percentage.

title: Tetro Domain
mechanics: turn-based territory claiming between two factions (blue vs pink) on a royal map
each turn, claim one vacant territory adjacent to the central castle or to land you own
any territory fully enclosed by your claims is captured automatically
some territories hold mines worth 1-3; the first to control a majority of total mine value wins
notes: A strategy game rather than an action Qix-like, but its enclosure capture rule is relevant. Posted 12 March 2026.

title: Pencil Pursuit
mechanics: side-scrolling runner across notebook pages, chased by the eraser; jump, freeze and weave through ink-drawn obstacles; five-continue budget
25 run pages in five chapters, each ending in a boss (Eraser, White-Out, Pen, Marker, Keyboard), then a 26th-page fight with the War Machine they build together
PENCIL REVENGE mode: fight pages that turn the chase on the rivals who chased you
REDRAW mode: 'draw your territory, close your lines, own the notebook' to claim the page (rules not detailed)
notes: Unreleased. Territory capture is a separate REDRAW mode with no published rules, not part of the fight pages.

title: Paint Tanks
mechanics: top-down tank shooter where bullets recolour map cells to your colour to capture area
opponents cannot drive on area you have captured, so territory is both terrain denial and an escape route
power-ups: bullet speed, bullet recolour area (2 cells per bullet instead of 1), reload time
up to 4 local players; you win only by eliminating the other players
notes: Free Godot game described as 'a game about capturing area and shooting'. The itch.io page shows no publish date.

title: Splash&Dash
mechanics: kart combat where every painted tile is claimed territory; most ground in your colour wins; rivals paint over you
drifting refills the paint tank
between rounds, pick cards that permanently upgrade your vehicle for the rest of the match; opponents build their decks too
vehicle classes: Heavies (ramming), Speedsters (fast cornering, wide trails), Standards (balanced); ram rivals off the map
arena power-ups such as speed boosts, paint bombs and shields; tracks change every lap
4-player local split-screen, 8 online; match length 2-10 minutes
notes: No line enclosure; listed for its territory loop with deckbuilding between rounds. Unreleased.

title: Gals Panic
publisher: Kaneko (export); Taito (Japan); Kaneko USA (US); Inter Trading (Korea); Saint-Fun (Taiwan)
mechanics: claimed areas reveal a hidden picture of a woman instead of a colour fill; the round clears at 80% of her silhouette, not 80% of the field
a 20-step meter (starting at 11) drifts toward a 'monster' side over time and jumps when large silhouette chunks are taken; claiming plain background pushes it back
with the meter low the picture becomes an unrelated monster image and finishing the round forces a replay; meter at 0 costs a life, meter at 20 clears the stage regardless of coverage
one boss per round: a spider that slows the player (round 1), a fireball (round 2), an electrified cuboid that clones itself (round 3), plus small enemies
alternating flip items: an angel raises the meter, a skull slows the player; an asteroid-storm symbol destroys enemies; 'loser' symbols turn the girl into a frog or octopus
a roulette after rounds 1 and 2 grants 1UP, BREAK or a dud for the next round; extra lives also come at score thresholds
6 girls x 3 rounds; the picture progresses each round and becomes a photo after the third; a 100% reveal shows a special clear screen
notes: Released November 1990. It founded the adult silhouette-reveal subgenre. About 10,000 units shipped worldwide (Gamemachine, 1990). The EXPRO-02 revision adds zoom effects and new Push Start and 100% Clear screens. The Korean edition swaps nudes for objects or animals, and the US version reportedly covers the girl in round 3. Kaneko also developed Super Qix (1987), but no checked source says Gals Panic reuses its engine or licenses Volfied's power-ups, so those claims were removed. An Android app 'Gals Panic' (com.knko.galpanic) exists on Google Play, but its developer and any link to Kaneko could not be confirmed.

title: LadyLove
mechanics: start menu: pick which of six models to play; each model has three levels whose backgrounds are her photos, uncovered as you cut
finishing a model's three levels unlocks a bonus photo, then returns you to model select with score and lives kept; no ending, play continues until the last life is lost
each of a model's three levels has its own animated main enemy: two different spiders (one fires a large web) and a spinning fire mass that forms a vortex
enemies do not move randomly: they often home toward the player's cutting point
an enemy touching the line being drawn erases that line and costs a life
per-level time limit (three minutes per old-games.ru)
keyboard-only: hold SHIFT while moving along the frame to cut into the picture
uncovering 80% auto-reveals the rest of the photo; larger single cuts score more
notes: Freeware per abandonwaredos.com (whose description text is unreliable and contradicts its own Qix-clone tag). old-games.ru tags it Japanese-developed, credits TPR as developer and publisher, and dates it 1991; LaunchBox and abandonwaredos give 1990. Starting lives conflict: five (LaunchBox) vs six (old-games.ru). MobyGames returns HTTP 403 to fetches, so it was not re-read.

title: Youjuu Club
alt_titles: Youjuu Club Custom (妖獣倶楽部カスタム, PC-98 collection of 1 and 2)
platforms: NEC PC-98 (1991-11-15, Youjuu Club Custom with Youjuu Club 2)
mechanics: the player's marker is a lecherous lesser demon uncovering a background image Xonix-style
a stage clears once 80% of the image is revealed
notes: An 18+ Japanese computer game and an early picture-reveal Xonix-like. VNDB tags it 'Xonix Game'. A sequel, Youjuu Club 2, came out on 1991-08-23.

title: Gals Panic II
publisher: Kaneko (arcade; Karam Trading licence in Korea); Mainichi Communications (Windows 95)
mechanics: an 8-way joystick allows diagonal lines
claiming starts from a rectangle inside the field and the player cannot connect to the outer border (kept by later entries)
the meter becomes time-based: revealing area no longer moves it
Quiz Version: each girl asks two-choice questions whose answers move the meter
a break-out mini-game after three rounds; clearing the blocks in time gives an extra life
an optional card dispenser (operator DIP switch)
Special Edition (1994): quiz removed, extra stages after the first clear, enemies that shoot, much harder
Windows 95 version: 30 stages in illustration and live-action modes with pyramid-style stage unlocking
notes: Released December 1993. The Quiz Version shipped first in Japan, and the later quiz-less Special Edition is the better-known release there. Refused classification in Australia (9 August 1996).

title: Perestroika Girls
mechanics: Super Qix hardware hack whose reward pictures are photos of women that grow more explicit over successive levels
gems give power-ups: shield, speed, time stop and others
bouncing hearts can be collected for points
the player can reverse along the line being drawn to erase it
two draw buttons, fast and slow
standing still too long sets a fire chasing along the player's line
claiming more than 80% reveals the whole picture
notes: MAME's superqix driver lists 'perestro' (Promat, 1994) and 'perestrof' (Promat, Fuuki license, 1993) as encrypted sets on no-MCU Super Qix hardware; the header calls it a hack of Super Qix. KLOV gives Promat/Fuuki, 1993. The earlier claim that it is a straight Super Qix rules clone with new pictures is not supported: LaunchBox describes gems, hearts and line erasing.

title: Cherry Bomb: Chou-ojou-sama Sayaka-chan Nanpa Daisakusen
alt_titles: チェリーボム 超お嬢さま沙也香ちゃんナンパ大作戦
CHERRY Bomb 超お嬢さま沙也香ちゃんナンパ大作戦
mechanics: adult adventure story framing with Xonix/Qix-style capture stages; per the VNDB tag, capturing enough of the screen reveals a hidden picture
notes: Adult title released on floppy on 7 April 1994 (VNDB release r59988). VNDB tags it 'Xonix Game' (alias 'Qix Game'). The tag definition is the only description of the capture stages, so their exact rules are unknown.

title: Fantasia
platforms: Arcade (Comad board derived from Kaneko's EXPRO-02)
mechanics: Gals Panic meter: the pointer creeps toward the monster side over time and jumps when big silhouette chunks are revealed; uncovering background pushes it back
a round finished while the monster image shows must be replayed
reveal 80% of the silhouette within a time limit while avoiding enemies
photographic Japanese and Western models instead of drawn art, with celebrity portraits as the bad images
notes: Released 7 March 1994. MAME has sets on 940307, 940429 and 940803 PCBs. It is the first of Comad's Gals Panic clones; MAME notes the Comad games derive from the EXPRO-02 Gals Panic, and Fantasia keeps encrypted tile ROMs and an extra layer. Two players, 8-way joystick. Portraits reportedly include Schwarzenegger, Bruce Willis, Michael Jackson, Peter Weller, Stallone and Harrison Ford.

title: Paradise
mechanics: Gals Panic-style silhouette reveal with photographs of nude Western models instead of drawn art
a bonus round triggered by the fill percentage when a stage is beaten
operator settings: fill target 75/80/85/90%, four round-timer settings, 3 or 5 lives, a slide-show mode
notes: Arcade-history calls it a rip-off of Gals Panic. The music rearranges the Lemmings soundtrack. Vertical screen, two players, 8-way joystick. MAME sets are Paradise set 1 and set 2 and an Escape-licensed set, on the YS-1600 board. Its sequel Paradise Deluxe is id 472.

title: Paradise Deluxe
mechanics: any of 12 stages can be picked at the start (16 stages in all)
reveal 80% of the silhouette to clear, 85% in later stages, while avoiding monsters
after each stage, under 90% revealed plays a roulette that can reward or punish; over 90% plays a four-card Monte with no penalty
each cleared stage removes a tile from a meta-picture, fully shown after all 16 stages
operator settings: fill target 75/80/85/90%, four round-timer settings, 3 or 5 lives, a slide-show mode
notes: Sequel to Paradise (1994), with Asian instead of Western models. Arcade-history calls it a rip-off of Gals Panic II. The year is not printed and MAME estimates 1994 or later (board YS-1604). Paradise 2 Deluxe (para2dx) is a separate MAME set that arcade-history calls a rehash with new Asian models. No separate 'Paradise 2' release was found, and the claim that 2 Deluxe is a censored version could not be checked. The original Paradise is a separate game (id 476).

title: SeXoniX
mechanics: each enclosed section reveals part of a picture of a suggestively posed woman, instead of the geometric fill patterns of earlier XoniX versions
notes: LaunchBox calls it a spin-off of the XoniX style (itself from Taito's Qix) in which claimed territory reveals images of suggestively posed women. The qixote wiki lists it in its Lewd section of porn-themed Qix clones. Adult phone games with similar names on mobiles24 ('Sexonix' 176x208 Java files, 'SexXonix - Russian Star 2' for S60v3) were uploaded by unrelated users. Nothing shows they are ports of this DOS game, so they were removed from this entry.

title: Spider
mechanics: the length of the line the player can draw is capped by the 'web power' available
bonus rounds where the player circles numbers as fast as possible
released in two sets, with and without nudity
notes: PCB found in Spain, apparently an original Spanish game. MAME's twins.cpp lists 'spider' (without nudity) and 'spidern' (with nudity), both Buena Vision 1994; the PCB is nearly identical to Twins but uses extra blitter features.

title: Double Strixx
mechanics: apparently a Laser Strixx evolution with added mini-games
notes: Not dumped. MAME's cubo.cpp known-games table dates it 1995; tilt.it gives '1996?'. In tilt.it's image, the attendants' faces are portraits of CD Express staff.

title: Gal Pani
mechanics: Qix-style capture reveals photographs of real models, including nudity, instead of drawn art
notes: A PC-9801 spinoff of the Gals Panic series. Not the same as Gal Pani II (1996, Mycom/Mainichi Communications), which is the PC-98/Windows 95 version of Gals Panic II.

title: Gals Panic 3
mechanics: a scrolling field larger than the screen; once a set share is revealed the view follows the cursor (introduced scrolling to the series)
the player chooses which girl to uncover before each stage
80% ends the stage; 100% unlocks a series of extra photos of that girl
mini-games between stages give a chance to win another girl's image
tighter time pressure and higher difficulty than the earlier games
uses only photographed (live-action) models
notes: Released October 1995 on its own Kaneko hardware (68000, YMZ280B; MAME galpani3, with Euro, Japan, Korea and Hong Kong sets). Japanese Wikipedia says exposure stops at underwear and early sales were poor. Refused classification in Australia (9 August 1996).

title: Harem Challenge
mechanics: 'rogue-qix' capture that uncovers a hidden photo
player energy meter; the operator sets the starting energy supply (100%, 50% or 0%)
operator option makes touching your own line deadly
area to cover: 75/80/85% for one player, 70/75/80% in two-player mode
level timer settable from 1:00 to 1:40
two-player tournament mode: best of 3 or best of 5
nine levels; the operator sets the photo grade (soft, erotic or explicit)
notes: Italy-only release: arcade-history says all CD Express games were released only in Italy. Mechanics come from Stephh's notes on the game's settings in MAME's cubo.cpp.

title: Laser Strixx
mechanics: photo uncovered fragment by fragment
skilled players unlock a striptease clip by a male or female performer
notes: Italy only. Not dumped: MAME's cubo.cpp lists it as known but undumped. tilt.it's heading names it 'Lucky Strixx' while its table says 'Laser Strixx', and it files the game in the 'rogue-qix' group.

title: Laser Strixx 2
mechanics: fence off territory to reveal a model photograph piece by piece
player energy meter; the operator sets the starting energy supply
operator option makes touching your own line deadly
nine levels
capturing a special 'mouth' object that appears during the level triggers a live-strip sequence at the end of the level
five performers (Ann, Eva, Jo, Sue, Bob) with 4 to 6 strip phases each
notes: Italy only. MAME emulates it as 'lasstixx'. Laser Strixx (1) and Double Strixx are listed in MAME as not dumped.

title: Zip & Zap
platforms: Arcade (Barko PCB 950509, derived from Kaneko EXPRO-02 / Comad design)
mechanics: Gals Panic-style silhouette capture that reveals a picture
optional 'Additional Obstacles' setting adds four blocker/bumper objects to the playfield
selectable player skill mode (Amateur, Normal, Excellent)
sold in two nudity grades: 'A' (Explicit) and 'B' (Less Explicit) ROM sets
character/stage select screen
notes: MAME groups it with the EXPRO-02 Gals Panic clones and says it is similar but could have other changes. The obstacle and skill-mode options come from MAME's DIP switch definitions. The earlier 'Korean' origin claim is not stated in the source and was dropped.

title: Dancing Eyes
mechanics: the field is the surface of a 3D polygon model covered in a grid of panels; clear every panel to finish the stage
player and enemies move only along fixed grid lines, so the player can be trapped between two enemies
touching an enemy that is on your own drawn line is not a miss
enemy types: slow mice and rabbits favouring different axes, fast squirrels, fish that shoot, snakes that charge, turtles that split, spiders that drop offspring, periodic starfish

items from glowing panels or flashing enemies: S speed, E extra time, T freezes enemies and the timer for 6 s, A giant invincible form, P stuns enemies touching your line, X/Y widen clearing horizontally or vertically, D clears many random panels and all enemies, W clears panels next to enclosed areas, R swaps cleared and uncleared panels, 1UP doll
time limit; fast clears earn a bonus reward scene
after each stage choose one of three next stages (41 stages in all)
most stages strip clothing from a woman model; others destroy UFOs, cardboard boxes or a cobra; the model poses and can be rotated after the clear
KIDS mode skips the undressing stages
notes: Released in Japan in September 1996; designer Masateru Umeda. Japanese Wikipedia says it builds on Qix and Volfied, and English Wikipedia's Qix page lists it as a 3D game similar to Gals Panic. A PS3 HD remaster (Namco Generations, PlayStation Move support) was announced in 2011 and cancelled on 26 April 2012.

title: Gal Pani II
developer: Scio (per LaunchBox); based on Kaneko's arcade Gals Panic II
mechanics: 30 stages in two switchable modes, illustration and live-action, with 15 stages each
illustration mode: five characters with three stages each
each mode has a five-tier pyramid stage-select map; clearing a stage opens the two stages below it
live-action mode reveals photographs of a single actress (Misako Maeda)
story frame: rescue girls held captive by monsters (the enemy bosses)
notes: Released 13 December 1996 through bookstores with an ISBN (4-89563-701-8). Japanese Wikipedia says it carried no age restriction, while LaunchBox says it includes nudity. Not an MS-DOS title.

title: Gals Panic 4
mechanics: bombs attack enemies and can wipe out the minor enemies on screen; revealing a large area in one capture awards more bombs
bombing an enemy in rapid succession adds status effects: slowed after the 3rd bomb, frozen in place after the 4th
2-player split-screen versus on separate pictures, where a bomb sends a sub-enemy to the opponent's side instead of attacking
7 girls x 3 stages (21 stages); 80% clears the stage, 100% plays a 'Showtime' interlude
two free mini-games playable during the attract demo
lower difficulty than earlier entries; rewards stop at swimsuits, with no nudity
notes: Released September 1996 in Japan. First Super Kaneko Nova title and the series' switch to anime-style art. EX, SU and DX are later Korean or Asian re-releases (MAME).

title: Paparazzi
mechanics: described by Arcade History as a rip-off of Mitchell's Lady Killer, itself a Gals Panic imitator; no detailed gameplay description found
round time limit set by operator (MAME 'Time' DIP: 80/100/120/150)
operator-selectable enemy set (MAME 'Enemies' DIP: Type 1 or Type 2)
two players simultaneous, 8-way joystick, one button
notes: Arcade Italia classes it as 'Puzzle / Misc.' and shows no explicit mature flag. The Qix-type play is inferred from the Lady Killer comparison and from the timer DIP, which matches other Gals Panic clones. Runs on Yun Sung 16-bit hardware (yunsun16.cpp), the same board as Shocking.

title: Pocket Gals V.I.P
mechanics: Gals Panic-style silhouette capture that reveals a picture (MAME groups it with the EXPRO-02 Gals Panic clones)
per-round play timer set by operator (70/80/100/120 seconds) with 6-10 lives (shared Gals Hustler input settings)
notes: MAME notes the ROMs carry Afega stickers and that the select screen looks wrong, so the dump may not be a final version. A 1997 second set of unknown manufacturer exists and is closer to Gals Hustler.

title: Sex Xonix (ZX Spectrum)
mechanics: Xonix-style capture with an adult picture theme
notes: Russian-language freeware. ZXDB lists Taito's Qix as its inspiration. ZXDB lists it as 'Sex Xonix [CENSORED]'. It appears to be a different game from the 1994 DOS SeXoniX.

title: Gals Hustler
developer: ACE International (ROMs also seen with Afega labels)
mechanics: Gals Panic-style silhouette capture that reveals a picture
per-round play timer set by operator (70/80/100/120 seconds) with 6-10 lives
notes: MAME describes it as possibly a hack of Pocket Gals V.I.P and notes an original PCB seen with genuine Afega labels. A hidden test mode (hold P2 button 1) exists but is not gameplay.

title: Gals Panic S - Extra Edition
mechanics: 'P' items power up the player, 'S' items raise movement speed
picking up a P item or claiming a large area in one capture lets the player shoot at the boss
attacking the boss too much enrages it: it then destroys already-claimed territory, and its attack kills even when the player is not drawing
all five EXTRA coins, which appear during captures, unlock an alternate, more risqué picture
80% clears the stage, 90% shows a nude still, 100% plays an animated 'SHOW TIME DX'
scrolling playfields, with some girls on fixed single screens
2-player versus on left and right halves: the first to claim 80% of the silhouette wins
11 women and one male character selectable, 12 stages; the male character moves around the select screen at random, so he is hard to avoid
notes: Released April 1997 in Japan. Start of the S series; much of the art is reused from Jan Jan Paradise.

title: Innai Kansen ~Mayonaka no Nurse Call~
alt_titles: 淫内感染 ～真夜中のナースコール～
mechanics: Xonix-style action stages (VNDB 'Xonix Game' tag); clearing a stage reveals an image and a short story scene
runs alongside the original Innai Kansen visual novel and adds two new characters
notes: Adult title, first released 4 Sep 1998. A picture-reveal action spin-off of a visual novel. Also included in the 2000 Collection Box and the 2014 'Premium Archives Mutou Keiji' compilation.

title: Lovely Girls
mechanics: claimed monster-free areas fill with part of a hidden photo of a model (75% target)
touching your own trail while drawing costs a life (respawn at top centre)
several monster types patrol both claimed and unclaimed areas: some follow the blue boundary lines, others hunt the line being drawn
extra life every 5,000 points (up to five lives at start)
per-level time limit that shrinks in later stages, with more aggressive enemies and new monster types
clearing a level shows the full high-resolution photo with manual or automatic pan and zoom
notes: Retro-replay lists the genre as Adult with a risqué theme; the Qixote wiki files it under its 'Lewd' clones. Lomax also published Hidden Fields (1995).

title: Vivid Dolls
mechanics: the player starts with a small claimed square inside a blurred image and draws lines outward from it, returning to claimed area to capture, instead of starting from the screen border
enemies act like 2D shooter enemies, each reacting differently, and some fire projectiles at the player; enemies break the line they touch
eight women with three images each; the last image is the most revealing
1-2 players
notes: Released December 1998 (Japan). MAME's aleck64.cpp lists 'vivdolls' (Visco, 1998).

title: Wonder Stick
mechanics: Amidar-style grid: the penguin draws a line only while the trace button is held, enclosing grid blocks; enclosed blocks vanish to reveal the image
each line starts with a tag that returns to the player when the button is released, or circles fully enclosed blocks to remove them
the moving tag kills enemies, which drop power-ups or food
a second button spends a 'help' (fish icon) to stun enemies briefly so you can pass them
enemy-free bonus stage every five levels to collect food and extra lives against a timer
operator DIP switch sets 3 or 5 helps
notes: Korean adult outline game; arcade-history gives a June 1998 release, while MAME dates it '????'. MAME has a second set labelled 'censored'. 68000 + Z80 hardware.

title: Gals Panic S2
mechanics: bosses get more attack patterns, so it is harder than S
some stages have two bosses at once, including the hidden character's stage
'Super Kaneko Dial': a phone icon appears on the stage and moves every so often; enclosing it gives that character's phone number after the stage
special phone numbers for clearing all stages, and for clearing all stages at 100%
12 women plus the hidden android character Nanako (775), 12 stages
2 players simultaneous, competitive
notes: The premium phone line has since closed. Seven of the 12 girls reuse art from VS Mahjong Otome Ryouran.

title: Land Breaker
mechanics: the player device moves freely inside the field instead of on its border
one button switches the cut between horizontal and vertical, and the other fires a laser both ways; the device can move again right after firing
a laser that crosses the field divides it, but the picture is revealed only in a part with no enemies; cuts with enemies on both sides stay as walls for herding enemies into smaller spaces
enemies are bouncing balls of several sizes, with more and smaller balls and less predictable movers in later stages
reveal at least 80% of the background against a timer; bonus points for the clear, for going above 80%, and for time left
items that are hit or trapped give immortality, faster beams, a magnet that freezes enemies, or an extra life
4 levels of 8 stages (32 stages)
notes: The Korean title 미스 땅짜르기 roughly means 'Miss Land-Cutting'. MAME lists three PCB versions (3.02, 3.03, 1.0), all from 1999. The hidden images are digitised photos of scantily clad women.

title: WOW Fantasia
mechanics: captured areas reveal a picture, as an entry in Comad's adult Qix-style Fantasia series (no title-specific gameplay details found)
notes: Known only from the Fantasia series list on Arcade History and Arcade Italia (Fantasia II and WOW New Fantasia pages). Not in MAME's expro02 driver, which has WOW New Fantasia (2002) but no 2001 'WOW Fantasia'. It may be undumped, or a series-list error.

title: Gals Panic S3
mechanics: stage select: girls fly in from the four corners to the centre until one is chosen
monsters attack with weapons; the enemy AI was changed and is harder than in S2
80% clears the stage; 90% shows a SHOWTIME image, 100% a static SHOWTIME DX image
8 stages
the Super Kaneko Dial phone feature was removed
gameplay largely reused from Panic Street (1999)
notes: Released July 2002. Kaneko's last arcade game and the last of the series. It was first planned as 'Gals Panic SP Print Daisakusen', which would print bonus images on a connected printer; that idea was dropped and S3 came out about a year later without it.

title: Miss World 2002
platforms: Arcade (Comad Fantasia II-type board, EXPRO-02 derived)
publisher: Comad; a Daigom-licensed set also exists
mechanics: Gals Panic-style silhouette capture revealing a picture; MAME rates the set at nudity grade 'A', the most explicit
two players simultaneously
notes: Runs on MAME's fantsia2 machine configuration and shares its sprite and sound ROMs with WOW New Fantasia. Sequel in the Miss World line to Miss World '96 Nude, which used photographs.

title: 女宇宙人触手陵○地獄
mechanics: Qix-type game in 3D (DLsite calls it a 'Qix-type 3D action puzzle')
story frame: Galactic Federation trainee Mizuho Kazami recovers her spaceship
10 stages
the reward CG tier depends on how well each stage is cleared
notes: DLsite release date: 28 December 2002. The circle mark in the title is DLsite's word masking.

title: Happy Tour
notes: MAME (hapytour) catver: Puzzle / Outline * Mature *, the class that holds Qix, Volfied and Gals Panic, so it is very likely a Qix-type adult-reveal game. No rules or gameplay description were found.

title: Yuukuri Panic Dokidoki Oyakodon
alt_titles: ゆーくりパニック どきどき親子丼
ゆ～くりパニック　どきどき親子丼

mechanics: grid capture on the Amidar model: the player can only move along rectangle borders and fills a rectangle by going all the way around it
filling rectangles uncovers a hidden picture underneath (a picture-reveal reward on a grid-capture board)
notes: Amidar clone in which the player is a robot. Mega Duck cartridge no. 028. Later included on Sachen multicarts (4-in-1 Version 6, the 31-in-1 Mighty Mix, and the 1999 Color 8-in-1 for GBC). The Mega Duck Wikipedia list only calls it 'a game similar to Pac-Man'; gamesdatabase.org describes the Amidar-style picture reveal.

title: Super Gal's Panic (Mega-CD)
notes: An unreleased prototype. arcade-history.com lists it under the 1990 Gals Panic! ports as a Mega-CD version called "Super Gal's Panic", an unreleased prototype. Wikipedia's Kaneko article lists it as "Super Gals Panic | 1994? | Sega CD | Unreleased" without a citation. Wikipedia's list of cancelled Sega CD games does not include it. No source describes its gameplay.

title: Gals Panic SS
mechanics: versus mode, added in the home port (not in the arcade Gals Panic 4)
the player can attack enemies, also new in the port
the clear goal is uncovering a glowing character silhouette, not a share of the whole field
notes: Released in Japan on 27 September 1996 and rated for all ages. It uses the Gals Panic 4 (4遊) system, and every character except Rito Tajima was redesigned. Kaneko's PlayStation release Silhouette Stories came out the same day. Famitsu scored it 25/40.

title: Silhouette Stories
alt_titles: シルエット☆ストーリィズ
publisher: Kaneko (GungHo Online Entertainment for the 2014 Game Archives release)
mechanics: story mode: pick one of 12 town locations to meet a girl; dialogue choices and stage results branch her story, and her true ending unlocks only after all her other endings
each stage has a random side objective (for example collect every item, or capture 30% of the area in one cut); failing it switches the story branch instead of ending the run
clear by uncovering 80% of the silhouette region, not of the whole field, so keeping the boss in a part with no silhouette is a valid strategy
one life and limited continues; a continue resets the current silhouette
pickup items such as a speed booster and a time stop
1-2 players
gallery of cleared images; finishing all of a girl's routes unlocks a dress-up mode
notes: Released in Japan on 27 September 1996, the same day as Gals Panic SS, with nearly identical play plus a light visual-novel story layer. It is based on Gals Panic 4 without the undressing element. GungHo re-released it on PS Game Archives on 5 November 2014. Famitsu scored it 23/40.

title: Live Wire!
mechanics: up to 4 players compete for the same grid at once (competitive territory instead of solo clearing)
claim a tile by drawing all four of its sides
power-ups steal tiles that opponents already own
a level ends when the timer runs out or every tile is captured
end-of-level score counts tiles held, tiles stolen and kills; the highest score wins the level
notes: Europe-only Amidar-inspired party game, released 10 April 1999. Reviews were mixed (Absolute PlayStation 74%, AllGame 3/5) and praised mainly the multiplayer. Music by Allister Whitehead.

title: Dino Master
alt_titles: 恐竜対戦 ダイノチャンプ 最強DNA発掘大作戦
Kyouryuu Taisen Daino Chanpu: Saikyou DNA Hakkutsu Daisakusen
mechanics: trace a line across a dig site; any fossil inside the closed line is uncovered (fossil reveal replaces the area quota)
an enemy that touches your open line sends a bullet along it toward you until it hits you or you reach a safe area (an enemy-triggered Fuse)
enemies enclosed by your line are destroyed
each level has a boss enemy that you must defeat to win the level

revived fossils become collectable dinosaurs with trade-offs (larger ones are stronger but have more weak points; the strongest are rarer) for a Battle Mode where you choose one of your dinosaur's parts to guard and one of the opponent's parts to attack
notes: Released in Japan on 22 Sep 2005, North America on 24 May 2006 and Europe on 27 Jun 2007. Wikipedia: 'similar to a fusion of Pokémon and the arcade game Qix'. The Japanese title comes from the Wikipedia article's note.

title: Critter Round-Up
mechanics: the farmer lays fences around a field to pen escaped animals and separate them by species
incompatible animals must be kept apart or they eat each other (e.g. a crocodile and a chicken in one pen)
aggressive animals and predators attack the farmer, so touching them must be avoided
presents fall from the sky with power-ups such as food that attracts animals or a spray that repels them
Adventure mode has 50 levels across five environments, each with its own species
endless Marathon mode for up to 4 players, co-operative or competitive
minigames: Snowball Soccer, Predator Rampage, Chicken Catch, Fence Trap
notes: Wikipedia says elements resemble Qix and that lead designer Brian Jury drew on Qix-style games. Nintendo Life calls it an 'animal-themed version of the classic arcade game Qix'. Released JP 25 Mar 2008, NA 19 May 2008, EU 29 Aug 2008.

title: Cubixx
platforms: PSP (PlayStation minis, also playable on PS3)
mechanics: the field is a cube: you cut segments off its six faces instead of a flat rectangle
each face has a droid that starts chasing your trail when you cut across its territory
from stage 2, light nodes run along the cube's edges and along cut edges (a Sparx analogue); a node trapped in a cut-off section disintegrates and reappears elsewhere
holding L or R while crossing a vertex chains faces into one cut; multi-face cuts multiply the score (risk/reward)
score comes from trail length, area claimed and faces crossed per run; enough points earn extra lives
you lose a life when a droid hits you or when you run into your own trail
the required percentage starts at 50% and rises every few levels; 20 levels
notes: EU PSN release on 17 Dec 2009 and US on 8 Jun 2010 ($3.99). Self-published by Laughing Jackal as a minis title. Followed by Cubixx HD (PS3, 2011).

title: Cubixx
publisher: Laughing Jackal; Ghostlight (Windows release of Cubixx HD)
mechanics: Qix-style capture moved onto the faces of a 3D cube
player robot (Cubot) fires a laser line across the cube to cut away and erase its sides
goal is to erase the cube's sides; enemies roam the cube and power-ups appear as levels progress
HD version: 50 arcade levels, 50 challenges, Score/Line/Time Attack modes
HD version: local co-op multiplayer and a Deathmatch versus mode
notes: Qixote's plain 'Cubix' is most likely a misspelling of Cubixx. No Qix-like game titled 'Cubix' was found. The 1991 Amiga Cubix (Xtreme D-Sign / media GmbH) is a puzzle game. The 1995 Scandere Cubix is a 3D strategy game. The 1998 and 2002 Cubix titles are cube-rotation and colour-swap puzzles, and the 2024 Steam Cubix (SandD) is a platformer. German Wikipedia's Qix article names AirXonix and Cubixx together as 3D variants, which matches Qixote's 'Air Xonix' and 'Cubix' in the same list. The original Cubixx is dated 2009 in the Cubixx HD article and 2010 in Laughing Jackal's article. Cubixx HD came out on PS3 on 17 Aug 2011 (EU) and 20 Sep 2011 (NA), and on Windows on 28 Jan 2016. Wikipedia reports a Metacritic score of 77, and Eurogamer called it the 'best reinvention' of Qix. Merge with any existing Cubixx or Cubixx HD entry.

title: Patchwork Heroes
mechanics: the field is an enemy warship: hold the cut button and draw a line fully across it, and the smaller severed side falls off
the HUD shows the percentage of the ship that remains
stage time limit; the timer pauses briefly in proportion to the share of the ship cut away
grey sections can only be destroyed with a mojo attack
the mojo gauge fills from cutting off parts, from items, or from using a bomb at the cost of allies; once triggered, a mojo attack slows your movement and lasts until the gauge empties
each bomb item blasts in its own direction
the R button blocks enemy attacks
allies are held in prisons on the ship: touch a prison to rescue them, and cutting it off before rescue loses them
game over when all allies are killed, when you are hit with no allies left, or when you enter a bomb's blast range
notes: Released in Japan on 18 Feb 2010 and in North America and Europe on 18 Mar 2010. Wikipedia: 'Similar in genre to Taito's Qix.' The main changes from Qix are dismantling a target against a clock and severing pieces instead of claiming area.

title: Urbanix
platforms: PSP (PlayStation minis, also playable on PS3)
mechanics: the player is a tractor that builds a town (houses) on the land it claims
the player's own trail is lethal: touching it costs a life, as does an enemy hitting it
capture takes a different number of passes per world: Town needs one, North Pole needs the snow cleared and then the land conquered (two), Moon Base needs three
Landrunners run from side to side without ever changing direction
Helisharks fly after the player; once caught, the player breaks free by mashing L and R (PSP) or shaking the Wii Remote (Wii), or loses a life
Housecrashers are harmless to the player but destroy the houses already built and must be chased away quickly
bonuses can be good or bad; the Wii review names speed boost, shield, extra lives and slowed time
a stage is cleared by filling a points gauge before a time limit runs out, and bigger enclosures score more
two-player co-op (WiiWare)
3 worlds of 50 levels each (150 in total)
notes: Nordcurrent's managing director announced the PSP minis release on the PlayStation Blog on 19 Oct 2010 and called it 'a mixture between Xonix and Qix'. The WiiWare release followed in January 2011 (EU 7 Jan, US 17 Jan). The Nordcurrent table on English Wikipedia lists iOS, PSP and Wii. The TouchArcade page for 'Urbanix Arcade' returned HTTP 403, so the iOS title could not be checked first-hand.

title: Cubixx HD
publisher: Laughing Jackal (presumed self-published; not stated in the review)
mechanics: new hazards on the cube-cutting base: Cubixx (small orange beings, the main early threat), Homers that latch onto your beam and cut its acceleration, asteroid showers, and Chasers that make the safe edge lines dangerous over time
Arcade mode of 50 stages unlocked in blocks of five, with the score carried through one session
Challenge mode replays each stage with alternative goals: score attack, line attack and timed challenges
competitive and co-op multiplayer for up to 7 players (split-screen)
notes: A full PS3 remake of the Cubixx minis title. EU release on 17 Aug 2011, US on 20 Sep 2011. The Push Square reviewer tested only four-player split-screen.

title: Dancing Eyes HD (cancelled)
mechanics: the playfield is a grid wrapped around a 3D character model; a monkey cuts panels away while avoiding enemies (from the 1996 arcade original)
PlayStation Move support announced
three announced character models: Crisitia Saietta, Francoise Mystere and Musaki Kikka
notes: An HD remake of Namco's 1996 arcade Dancing Eyes, announced as a PS3 exclusive in the Namco Generations line with Pac-Man Championship and Galaga Legions. Cancelled for unknown reasons. English Wikipedia lists Dancing Eyes among the Gals Panic clones.

title: Poison Control
mechanics: Qix-style enclosure inside a third-person shooter / action RPG: areas of poison swamp must be encircled ('rounded off') to purify and beat them
notes: Released in Japan on 25 Jun 2020, North America on 13 Apr 2021 and Europe on 16 Apr 2021. Wikipedia lists the genre as action role-playing and says it 'has been compared to a fusion of a third-person shooter and Qix'. The campaign has five major areas (Belles' Hells). The precise enclosure controls and their effect on enemies were not verified.

title: Ink & Paper: DoodleCut
mechanics: a doodle bug draws a line behind it on a notebook page; enclosed areas get doodled (claimed)
capture more than three-quarters of the page to win
levels add special areas and several enemy types
enemies kill you by catching you or by cutting your open line
2-player local co-op, scored on most space in the shortest time
unlockable expert speed and endless mode
notes: Released on the EU eShop on 24 Feb 2023. naptime.games Sp. z o.o. (Poland) is the publisher and copyright holder; no separate developer is listed. Its shared 'cut your line' wording with Pet Show (another Polish Switch Qix) is not evidence of a shared engine.

title: XPOSED SWITCHED
mechanics: captures are drawn as rectangles only, uncovering the hidden background; expose enough of it to clear the level
3 terrain types, each with its own hazards
4 power-ups that appear at random during play
8 enemy types
48 levels
notes: Released standalone on the US eShop on 20 Jan 2023 (single player). Re-sold in 2024 in the Arcade Fusion Bundle with The Crystals of Atlantis (EU eShop, 23 Apr 2024).

title: Pet Show
developer: LUKAVERSE (co-copyright holder with QubicGames; no developer credit on store pages)
mechanics: closing your line reveals part of a hidden pet picture
flying foes and bugs that hit your open line before you close it cost you a life
screen-edge teleporting (wrap-around) and speed boosts help you dodge
48 stages, each with 3 difficulty options
2-player local co-op uncovering the same picture
notes: Released on 5 Jul 2025 (EU and US eShop). A family-friendly picture-reveal Qix. Copyright: © 2025 QubicGames S.A. and © 2025 LUKAVERSE sp. z o.o.

title: Invincible Little Warrior
platforms: unnamed 'DDR' dance-mat plug & play consoles (HDMI output, sold under names such as "FWFX Dance Mat")
developer: Shenzhen Niutai Technology Development Co., Ltd (China)
mechanics: Gals Panic-style picture reveal whose backgrounds show anime characters such as Luffy and Doraemon
notes: An unlicensed Chinese plug-and-play game. Niutai often went uncredited, so the wiki says attribution is hard to confirm. Niutai traded under that name from 2006 to January 2020.

title: Jintori Action! Taikōkenchi: Karakuri Shiro no Nazo
alt_titles: Jintori Action! Taikoukenchi - Karakuri Shiro no Nazo
mechanics: gameplay details unverified; 'jintori' (陣取り) is the Japanese genre term for Qix-style territory-taking games, and 'Taikō kenchi' (Hideyoshi's land survey) suggests a land-claiming theme
notes: Japan-only WiiWare title, listed on Wikipedia's WiiWare list (credit: Perpetuum, Japan only) and in the No-Intro Wii (Digital) dat as 'Jintori Action! Taikoukenchi - Karakuri Shiro no Nazo (Japan) (WiiWare)'. Release date and gameplay not found. Qix lineage is inferred from the title.

title: Protean Girl
developer: Fuzhou Waixing Computer Science & Technology Co., Ltd (China)
mechanics: Gals Panic-style picture reveal whose backgrounds are eroge characters, mostly clothed
notes: An unlicensed Chinese plug-and-play game, listed under the games Waixing produced itself. The wiki calls it uncommon because of its risqué content. One first-stage image shows Amatsue Hikari from Dyogrammaton.

title: Just4Qix
publisher: freeware (Dingux release; Amiga port on Aminet)
mechanics: claimed area uncovers a hidden background picture (one of ten backgrounds), Gals Panic style
level clears above 80% coverage
the boss bounces freely across the whole screen and never kills the player by touch

when the boss crosses a drawn track line it can spawn fire 'henchmen' that run along the track lines and steer toward the player's current trail; touching one costs a life, followed by 3 seconds of invulnerability
per the README, completing a fill while a fire is on your tail douses it
notes: Version 0.1 was first released for Dingux on the Dingoo A320, dated 17/10/2009. README.DINGOO calls it 'a little bit of phun inspired by Gals Panic'. Lorence Lombardo compiled the Amiga 68k build and uploaded it to Aminet on 2012-12-18, with C/SDL source included (src.7z). The boss, henchman and reveal-overlay behaviour comes from that source (update.c, render.c).

title: JezzBall (PICO-8, roywig)
notes: Straight 'play-alike' of the Windows game, posted as v0.8 on 30 December 2016. The author says the flood fill is subtly broken: it sometimes fails or runs slowly. Collision detection is imperfect but usually favours the player.

title: JezzBall (Gamebuino / Arduboy)
developer: ThomasPietrzak on GitHub, credited as RackhamLeNoir in the Arduboy Collection; Arduboy adaptation by akkera102
notes: Straight clone, described in the README as a tribute to the TI-89 JezzBall the author played for hours. GPL-3.0; built with the Arduino IDE and the Gamebuino library. Commits run from 6 April 2017 to 13 October 2018. akkera102 adapted it to the Arduboy using the Gamebuino library, dated 31 October 2017 in the Arduboy Collection.

title: Cellonix
mechanics: the goal is stated as filling the whole board
enemies crawl both inside the board and outside it
points raise a persistent rank, and each rank increases movement speed
achievements for specific tasks award extra points
the Premium Edition adds special skills and difficulty levels
notes: A PICO-8 game released on 5 Apr 2019; version 2.0.1 came out on 22 Dec 2019 and added profile saves, level restart and tips. The Free Edition has normal difficulty only, 20 levels, a rank cap of 5 and 12 of 20 achievements. The Premium Edition costs at least $2.99 and adds more levels, special skills and difficulties. English and Polish.

title: Stix (PICO-8)
publisher: pahammond (self-published on itch.io, name your own price)
mechanics: goal: trap the energy bundle by filling 75% of the arena
one action button (X) to leave the grid and draw
fuses move fast (players say so in the comments, and the author acknowledges it)
