notes: The author calls it 'my Pico-8 interpretation of the Qix arcade game and the C64 Stix game'. v0.80 was released in 2019 (exact day not given). v0.81 (17 Nov 2023) added a custom font, and binaries followed in a 20 Nov 2023 devlog. The author also says it was their second PICO-8 game and that it adapts line-based graphics to PICO-8's low resolution.

title: ISOL8: Build & Isolate
mechanics: level is won when every ball is walled off from every other ball, checked by flood fill, rather than by reaching an area percentage
player builds horizontal or vertical walls; a ball hitting a wall under construction costs a life
one more ball each level, up to 15
choice of 1, 3 or 5 lives (listed as Easy, Normal, Hard), plus an Endless mode where you cannot die
background and ball palettes change every 5 levels; colours are random every level after level 100
guide lines show where the wall will be built (v3), and an alternate control scheme (hold a button, then pick the direction)
notes: Posted 20 August 2021 and updated to v3 on 25 August 2021. Originally designed for the Playdate, where turning the crank built walls. The author's first PICO-8 game. The isolation win condition is a distinct capture rule.

title: Paper-io (MakeCode Arcade)
mechanics: offline single-player Paper.io clone: one human snake, bots spawn every 2 seconds until 6 snakes are on the map
leaving your colour draws a trail; returning traces your outer boundary and flood-fills it, overwriting rival colour inside
the snake that runs into any trail, its own or a rival's, dies, not the trail's owner (reversed from Paper.io)
hitting the map wall kills; a snake whose territory is reduced to zero tiles dies
a dead snake's territory is wiped back to empty and its colour returns to the spawn pool
bots make random 90-degree turns, a few per excursion
result screen shows time alive and percent of the map claimed; leaderboard bars and a minimap
notes: TypeScript/Blocks project for the MakeCode Arcade editor, written May 2021 (commits from 13 to 19 May 2021). Behaviour checked in main.ts.

title: JEZZAK
publisher: Optimal Prime Futureworks LLC (itch.io and Playdate Catalog)
mechanics: goal: capture over 80% of the play area while indestructible 'Ultra Dense Spheres' and other enemies bounce around
player avatar moves with the D-pad; B rotates it and A extends the 'isolator' wall
cranking forward overcharges the isolator so walls build faster; too much overcharge makes the player explode
power-ups deployed with A+B or by cranking backward, e.g. lightning and snail to deal with fast balls, chaff to counter seeker missiles
seeker missiles that cannot pass through screen edges and must arc back toward the player
30+ ball, enemy and power-up types
story episodes with unique locations, bosses and animated cutscenes; 50+ levels
2 arcade modes, including 'Arcade Classic', added on request to play closer to JezzBall
scoreboard and playable credits
notes: Area-capture game 'similar to Qix, Jezzball, or Barrack', with an alien-invasion story. $3. The itch.io devlog dates v1.0.1 (adds Arcade Mode) to 3 September 2023; the Playdate Catalog lists it as first published 11/07/2023. The store page lists 3 episodes, but per itch.io comments Episode 3 is 'Lost Levels' and a planned second story episode was not finished. Seeker-missile, chaff, lightning and snail details come from the developer's comments, not the store text.

title: Stix Disruption
publisher: pahammond (self-published on itch.io, name your own price)
mechanics: hold X while leaving the trail to draw at half speed for a 'bonus 2x' fill; release it at once for a normal fill
2-player co-op: player 2 shoots the Stix to 'disrupt' it, which the page warns may make it more unpredictable
fast fuse: players report it, and the author says it carried over from the PICO-8 Stix
notes: A Picotron sequel to the author's PICO-8 Stix, distributed as stix.p64.png plus exported binaries. v0.80 was released 17 Sep 2024, and the binaries were rebuilt 14 Apr 2026. One button (X) both leaves the grid and fires.

title: Xonix (PICO-8)
mechanics: 75% land to clear a level
a land enemy patrols claimed land, and each time the level timer runs out another land enemy spawns
one more sea enemy each level (starting at 3)
3 lives; score equals the number of cells captured
notes: A straight Xonix clone on a 64x61 grid. A pocket is not filled if it contains a sea enemy. Commits run from 30 May to 12 June 2024. The mechanics come from xonix.p8.

title: Q*BALL
mechanics: playfield is a Q*bert-style isometric pyramid of cubes the player hops across
hopping marks horizontal or diagonal lines of cubes, and marked lines drop out of play
blocks cut off from both the player and the q*balls slowly decay (capture by isolation)
randomly bouncing q*balls undo your progress, so you must trap them
clear at least 16 blocks per level against a timer; pressing X speeds the timer up to advance sooner
whole game fits in 1020 compressed bytes, with all sprites generated by code
notes: Pico-1k 2025 jam entry (posted 25 September 2025), 'inspired by q*bert and jezzball'. The BBS links out to play at lexaloffle rather than embedding the cart.

title: OVERWORLD
mechanics: holding A or B changes movement speed and stops the trail from solidifying while held: finer control and more bonus area, at the cost of longer exposure to enemies
territory captured beyond the level target scores bonus points
collecting enough bonus earns bonus items
notes: A 1-bit, Halloween-themed action-puzzle inspired by AirXonix. Published on itch.io on 30 Oct 2026 and still in development. The Playdate build is sideloaded; the browser build runs on the wasmoon Lua VM. AI-assisted code; Artem Tyurin contributed a non-recursive flood fill. An open-world mode is planned but not implemented.

title: Moss Covers Everything
mechanics: the player (a moss ball) always moves forward; two buttons only turn left or right, Snake-style
every square crossed becomes moss, and closing a loop of moss fills the enclosed interior too
enemies caught inside filled moss are deactivated and become harmless pushable skulls
pushing a deactivated skull into a bug destroys the bug, so captures double as ammunition
level goal is to cover the crystal with moss, not to reach a coverage percentage
notes: Short PICO-8 puzzle prototype set in a dungeon, with a title screen and ending but no sound; the author notes some movement bugs. Tagged 'qix' on itch.io. No date is shown on the page; its low itch.io game id (48307) points to an early upload (around 2016), but this is not confirmed.

title: TIXONIX
mechanics: level n starts with n+1 balls bouncing in the unclaimed area, plus one enemy that bounces only inside claimed land
a 60-second countdown on the HUD spawns one more land enemy each time it runs out; losing a life removes the extra land enemies and restarts the countdown
capturing past the 75% goal pays a bonus of 50 points for each percent of the goal above 100
score is 1 point per enclosed cell; trail cells count toward the goal but score nothing
game logic steps every third frame and sprites are drawn between cells, which gives the smooth movement
notes: A Lua cart on an 80x42-cell field with a 75% goal and 3 lives. The author says Xonix was played on Soviet PC XT clones, found no playable remake, and made this one. The page credits the original DOS game to Ilan Raab and Dani Katz (1984). Commenters compare it to Go Hamster!. The mechanics were read from the cart's Lua source.

title: ZUBGUBBLERS
developer: ROBYSOFT (Nick Santaniello); music by Devin Curry (Grand Atrium)
publisher: ROBYSOFT (self-published on itch.io, name your own price)
mechanics: four local players (best with 4 gamepads) race to cover the playfield in their own colour and pattern
power-ups to collect and 'nefarious powerdowns' to avoid
players can sabotage opponents
very short rounds (itch lists the average session as 'a few seconds')
notes: A minimalist, abstract PICO-8 party game. The author tagged it 'qix' on itch.io, but the page does not say whether painting works by enclosing area or by covering cells directly. No publish date is shown. Its itch game id (723491) suggests about 2020, which is an estimate only. robysoft.net is now a parked domain.

title: Zoid
year: early 1980s (unpublished; written while Cohen was in high school, which he finished in 1984)
notes: In IEEE Spectrum, Cohen says he wrote 'a video game I called Zoid' in 6502 assembly on an Apple II Plus. It used digitized speech of him saying 'Zoid', slowed down, and he tried to sell it to Broderbund. He says it 'was played heavily by me and my father and no one else'. The Qix connection rests on MobyGames trivia (seen by the research agent; MobyGames returned 403 to me) and the Qixote listing; the interview gives no gameplay details.

title: Graphic QIX
publisher: Compaq (as listed by MAME); published in 'Maikon Game no Hon 3' (Kohgakusha)
notes: MAME's pc8801_cass.xml lists it among known undumped N-BASIC games, dated July 1982, which makes it one of the earliest Japanese home-computer Qix versions. No dump exists, so its gameplay is undocumented.

title: Jeepers Creepers
mechanics: irregular grid of rectangles of varying sizes; recolouring all lines around a rectangle captures it, and the level ends when every line is coloured
four named mazes: Number One, Scrambler, Brick Wall, Skull Run
power-ups hidden in some rectangles and gained on capture: a jump that teleports the bug to a random point of the maze
Beetle power-up: a beetle hunts one wasp and removes it on contact
Super Beetle: 1-3 unmarked rectangles per level hide a faster beetle that eats several wasps
optional 'coast' movement keeps the bug sliding along its path after the joystick is released
wasps patrol the grid as enemies
notes: Written in QS Forth, which Albanese also wrote and Quality Software sold. Its random-teleport jump replaces Amidar's jump over enemies.

title: Kid Grid
mechanics: capture all 35 squares of a fixed grid by turning all four of their sides from dotted to solid
four pursuers (Moose, Squashface, Muggy, Thuggy) that look different but behave identically
question marks appear at random in squares and give bonus points when that square is captured
limited stun button briefly freezes the enemies so the player can pass through them (stand-in for Amidar's jump)
selectable 3, 5 or 7 stuns per game and five difficulty levels
notes: Heavily borrows from Amidar. GameBase 64 credits Arti Haroutunian for the C64 version too, lists a high-score saver, and links a sequel, 'Kid Grid II - Kid vs. Kid'.

title: Night Flight
mechanics: a plane flies over a city leaving a trail, and closing a rectangle fills it
a lightning bolt sent by a thunder god chases you, and trapping it inside your filled area clears the level
shooting stars cross the screen now and then as extra hazards
an enemy touching the unfinished trail destroys the plane
parachute bonus scene: steer a passing plane to catch your falling pilot for an extra life
2 players alternating
notes: Pyuta ROM No. 7, described as a 陣取りゲーム (territory-capture game). Generation MSX notes the Pyuta title screen reads 1982, while LaunchBox gives 1983. Wikipedia's Tomy Tutor article lists it as Japan-exclusive. The Italian pirate magazine Linguaggio Macchina MSX 09 (February 1988) distributed it as 'Qix'.

title: Time Runner
developer: Yves Lempereur; C64 port by Scott Maxwell and Troy Lyndon
mechanics: claim 20 rectangular boxes on a checkerboard field by tracing their edges
two grid types alternate by phase: in one, a bonus counter drains while you trace and you keep what remains when every line is covered
in the other grid type each box has its own point value, which starts draining once two of its sides are traced and stops when the box is closed
the number of chasers grows with each phase
three uses per game of a key that briefly paralyses all pursuers
at set moments the chasers go blind and can be run into for extra points
extra life every 10,000 points
notes: Reviewers compared it to Amidar, and 80 Micro (April 1983) called it non-violent. Wikipedia's lead says 1981, but its release table and the reviews say 1982 for the TRS-80 and Atari, and GameBase 64 says 1983 for the C64. WizardSoft's C64 'Blade Runner' is listed as a clone of it.

title: Colour Clash
mechanics: Amidar-style grid painting; no source describes its mechanics in detail
notes: Spectrum Computing lists Amidar as its inspiration and Currah MicroSpeech support. Sinclair User gave it 4/10 (a 40% average). Covertape releases: 'Rodillo' (Software Magazine #16, 1985) and an unauthorised 'Pennellix' (Load 'n' Run #9, 1984). Wikipedia's list misspells the publisher as 'Romnik'.

title: Crazy Painter (Superior Software)
mechanics: Amidar-style grid painting; no source describes its mechanics in detail
notes: An early pre-release titled 'Amidar' circulated on the 8BS public-domain disc TBI-193 ('PD Games #11'). The game was later included in Superior Collection Volume 2.

title: Crazy Tracer
mechanics: Amidar clone: the player traces the edges of a fixed rectangular lattice instead of cutting free-form areas, and a rectangle fills once its whole perimeter is traced
notes: bbcmicro.co.uk: 'Crazy Tracer is a clone of the 1981 arcade game Amidar from Konami', genre Maze with secondary genre Amidar, Model B only, joystick optional. Walter Mansell also wrote Frenzy (Micro Power, 1983), which bbcmicro.co.uk files under the secondary genre Qix.

title: Cuthbert Goes Walkabout
mechanics: fill every square of a grid while avoiding monsters
each level has a time limit; the grid must be finished before time runs out
notes: Based on Amidar. Part of the Cuthbert series. Wikipedia also lists Microdeal as developer.

title: Damper
mechanics: move around a power grid filling in squares; the database likens it to Zolyx with fixed pathways
notes: Spectrum Computing records it as based on Amidar. It was re-released in 1983 on a double tape with Glooper. Sinclair User gave it 7/10. The Zolyx comparison is a modern database description, since Zolyx came later.

title: Demon Decorator
mechanics: Amidar-style grid painting; no source describes its mechanics in detail
notes: First released as 'Painter' and renamed, possibly to avoid confusion with A&F's Painter. Included on the compilation Micro Power Magic 3. No author is credited.

title: Fill 'Er Up!
publisher: ANALOG Computing (type-in, issue 10, Feb/Mar 1983); Calisto Software and A1 (Electric Starfish, UK); QuelleSoft (Starkstrom Seestern, Germany, 1984)
mechanics: no border-running sparks at all
a single drawing speed, without Qix's two-speed, two-point drawing
notes: A magazine type-in distributed as a BASIC listing of machine code. Tom Hudson says Electric Starfish was an unauthorized copy with another author's name added. Commenters recall a glitch that filled the whole screen at once. Both mechanics come from Atarimania user comments.

title: Fill 'Er Up! II
publisher: ANALOG Computing (The ANALOG Compendium book, ISBN 0-914177-00-1)
mechanics: adds enemy sparklers that burn like fuses along the walls, which the first version lacked
notes: The ANALOG Compendium calls it a 'slightly updated release' of Fill 'Er Up!. The sparkler addition comes only from Atarimania user comments.

title: Gridder
mechanics: trace the edges of each square to recolour it; the whole grid must be coloured
some areas start already coloured solid and hide the player from chasers, so they work as shields
chasers see the player only when on the same line, or when crossing the line the player is crossing
fire button leaves a hole in the player's wake, which does not work when a chaser is right behind
each grid has a time limit, and remaining time is added to the score
3 lives per grid, with extra lives carried over up to 9; 256 grids
notes: Electronic Games reviewed the VIC-20 cassette (July 1984, p. 30). GameBase 64 lists a 1983 C64 Gridder by Microdigital, programmed by R.W. Stevens, with the comment 'C= Games 2001 Nr. 1 / a.k.a. "Squares"'. The same programmer made Terminal Software's C64 Super Gridder. The review does not say what the hole does to chasers.

title: Oh Mummy
mechanics: the player leaves a footprint trail, and fully enclosing a tomb box with footprints reveals its content: scroll, mummy, key, tomb, or nothing
a level is cleared only after both the key and the tomb are uncovered
a scroll lets the player kill one mummy on that level
an uncovered mummy chases the player and carries over to the next level
speed and difficulty rise each level
turn-based multiplayer where players alternate levels
notes: A clear example of captured boxes hiding items that can help or hurt. Amsoft's CPC version was often bundled with the computer, and the Spectrum version was in the 1986 ZX Spectrum 128K +2 introductory bundle. Spectrum Computing lists it under Amidar. The music is based on 'The Streets of Cairo'.

title: Painter (A'n'F Software)
mechanics: maze painting after Make Trax / Amidar; no source describes its mechanics in detail
notes: Spectrum Computing lists it as inspired by Make Trax, and the BBC Micro site files it under the Amidar genre. Reviewed in Home Computing Weekly (Apr 1983) and ZX Computing (Aug 1983).

title: Potty Painter
mechanics: join dotted lines around squares of different sizes; each square is worth different points
5 lives and 3 freezes; each freeze stops the enemies for about 10 seconds
levels alternate between two themes: a monkey vs tribesmen and a paint roller vs teddy bears
bonus round after a level: guide a teddy bear to a banana for 1,000 points
notes: Released December 1983 and described as an Amidar clone. Spectrum Computing's Amidar licence list includes it. The Wikipedia article is a stub.

title: Qix (VIC-20, Wizardsoft)
notes: Known only from an uncited row 'Qix (aka Squeeze) || 1983 || Wizardsoft' in Wikipedia's List of VIC-20 games. Its gameplay is undocumented.

title: RollerBall
mechanics: the Qix is a single bouncing ball, trapped by claiming 75% or more of the field
two 'Squeezer' enemies patrol the outlines of filled areas
touching your own trail costs a life
notes: The player draws with a 'space scriber'. Not the pinball game of the same name.

title: Rollin
publisher: Scand Soft (1983 original); Atlantis Software Ltd. (UK release, 1984 per GameBase 64)
mechanics: Amidar-model grid capture: the player traces the edges of a fixed rectangular lattice instead of cutting free-form areas, and a cell fills once its whole perimeter is traced (inferred from the GameBase 64 genre 'Arcade - Amidar'; no gameplay text found)
notes: GameBase 64 has two entries: a 1983 release by Scand Soft (Swedish) and a 1984 release by Atlantis Software Ltd. Both credit Micke Nordström for code, music and graphics. The Wikipedia list's '1983, Atlantis' mixes the two releases. Lemon64 (Wikipedia's citation) returned 403 and could not be checked.

title: Stix
publisher: Supersoft (C64, BBC); Audiogenic (BBC); Keypunch Software (Kwixx, C64, 1985)
mechanics: Quark and anti-quark enemies walk the inner border of finished fields and destroy the synthesizer on contact
stopping too long while drawing builds up energy until the synthesizer explodes
finite fuel supply for the synthesizer
holding fire draws slower and scores 20 points per 1% instead of 2
leaving less area to Stix at level end scores more
75% clears a level
a timer: running out ends the game regardless of lives, and losing a life refills it
caught while drawing, you restart where the line began, and a nearby quark can cost another life at once
player-adjustable movement speed (cursor up/down slower, left/right faster)
notes: Circulated as 'Qix' or 'Quix' in PD libraries and on Zzap!64 Megatape #35 (October 1992). Keypunch re-released it in 1985 as Kwixx in the Arcade Games II pack. The BBC version is on the Power Pack vol. 1 and vol. 2 compilations.

title: Styx
mechanics: 8-way movement: Stix can be drawn diagonally, not only orthogonally
stopping or leaving a line unfinished is fatal (HOTU: the Fuse catches you)
the border enemy is a dotted 'caterpillar' (Sparx equivalent) that is faster than in the arcade; a second one runs the opposite way from level 2
from level 4 the caterpillars grow longer continuously; one trapped in a filled area, or a lost life, resets them to small size
from level 3 there are two smaller, slower Styx, and separating them makes one disappear
the score multiplier cycles over time by colour (blue 1x, red 5x, green 10x points per 0.1% filled), so timing a claim matters
80% clears a level, with a 1,000-point bonus per full percent above 80%
notes: Released on a copy-protected bootable floppy that needs a genuine CGA card. Source code released in September 2004, and Andrew Jenner's 1998 Styx Remastered runs on modern PCs. Home of the Underdogs gives a 65% clear threshold, but the rules page of the official remaster site gives 80%, which the bonus rule depends on. digger.org also says trapping one of the two Styx roughly halves the player's speed.

title: Super Gridder
mechanics: Amidar-style grid capture (GameBase 64 genre tag); no source describes its mechanics in detail
notes: GameBase 64 lists it as 1983, Terminal Software, programmed by R.W. Stevens, with 'Gridder' (Microdigital) as a related game. It is probably an enhanced C64 version of Gridder, but that is not confirmed. Wikipedia lists it without a citation.

title: Traxx
mechanics: paint every section of a rectangular grid by moving along it; the level ends when the whole grid is painted
unlike Amidar, rectangles are not filled when surrounded, so only line coverage counts
options set the game speed and the number of enemies on screen
notes: An early Jeff Minter design in the Amidar family, also listed among Llamasoft's 8-bit games. Wikipedia's infobox lists single- and multiplayer modes, but the article does not describe multiplayer, so it was removed from the mechanics.

title: Xonix (Apple II, Matthias Gerhardt)
developer: Matthias Gerhardt (the disk spells it 'MATTHIAS GERHARDT' and 'M.GERHARDT'; Wikipedia's 'Matthais' is a typo)
publisher: none credited on the disk (no commercial publisher found; it circulated on compilation disks)
mechanics: area capture tracked by an AREA counter on the HUD ('SCORE 00000 -- AREA 000 - STICKS 2')
lives shown as 'STICKS', a possible nod to Qix's Stix
high-score table ('HISCORE TRY IT !!')
notes: The game exists and its author and date are confirmed by primary disk images in the Asimov Apple II archive. In the 'Xonix, Pooyan' disk, the XONIX binary holds the string '(C) BY  M.GERHARDT>>1983<<' and the status line 'SCORE 00000 -- AREA 000 - STICKS 2'. A BASIC loader prints '*** XONIX ***', 'WRITTEN AND CREATED BY MATTHIAS GERHARDT'. The same binary, with the same credit string, sits on an Italian compilation disk whose menu is dated 8/8/1990 ('GIOCHI VARI'). That disk is 'Lucrezia_Xonix_RasterBlaster'. The 1983 copyright date comes before the 1984 IBM PC Xonix by Ilan Rav and Dani Katz, so the name was already used on the Apple II a year earlier. Gameplay was not watched in an emulator. The area-claiming core is inferred from the title and the AREA percentage field on the HUD. Whether it follows the Xonix rules, with enemies both on the sea and on the land, or the Qix rules is not confirmed. The archive also holds an unrelated, uncredited Apple II XONIX disk (unsorted/XONIX.DSK). Its leftover assembly source has 'INCR COUNT & %TAGE', 'FLAG75' (probably a 75% clear threshold) and 'COPY MAP TO HGR2', so it is a second Apple II Xonix-style implementation. No web search could be run: the web-search budget was used up. The evidence comes from fetching the archive's files directly.

title: Doodlebug
publisher: A&B Computing (Argus Specialist Publications), January/February 1984 type-in
mechanics: you draw rectangles up from the filled bottom of the screen; a finished rectangle fills its whole bounding box down to the floor, and the level is won when the fill reaches the top of the screen
score per rectangle grows with its height and width and is multiplied by the level number
the Bug bounces around the open area and kills you only if it touches the line of an unfinished rectangle; at higher levels it turns towards your cursor more often
Blips (from level 2): a 10-step countdown (about 2.5 s) starts at random, more often at higher levels, and you lose if you do not finish a rectangle before it ends
no lives: a failure divides the score by 1.5 and replays the level, and a cleared screen multiplies the score by 1.5 and moves you up a level
notes: Mechanics come from the game's own instruction screens and BASIC listing on the bbcmicro.co.uk disc image. The instructions say to fill 'around 90%', but the code tests for a filled top row.

title: Frenzy
mechanics: the smaller enclosed area is always the one filled, so Leptons trapped there are killed
levels usually end by killing all Leptons rather than by reaching a percentage; all count as captured once 95% of the screen is filled
Leptons move in regular, deterministic patterns
Chasers on higher levels kill the craft on contact
the craft can pause briefly
2x score multiplier for areas filled using only the slow speed
extra craft after screens 3, 6 and 9
up to five Leptons and five Chasers; levels 12 and 14 have fewer but much faster Leptons and no Chasers
14 unique levels, after which the last two screens repeat indefinitely
notes: The capture-kills-enemies rule is the key departure from Qix. bbcmicro.co.uk dates the BBC version 1983, but Wikipedia gives 1984, consistent with an August 1984 Acorn User review. GB64 dates the C64 version 1984, Wikipedia 1985. GB64 links the Italian 'Fotone' (Super Game 2000 No. 12, February 1986, Pubblirome) to Frenzy as a clone.

title: Hooper
mechanics: Amidar-model grid capture: trace the edges of a fixed rectangular lattice, and a cell fills once its whole perimeter is traced (inferred from the GameBase 64 genre 'Arcade - Amidar'; no gameplay text found)
notes: GameBase 64: programmer Mak Jukic, genre 'Arcade - Amidar', single player, joystick in port 2.

title: Painting Joe
mechanics: Amidar-inspired grid painting (Spectrum Computing lists Amidar as its inspiration; no gameplay description found)
notes: French-language, single player, beeper music, redefinable keys. Two files exist: a 'Gameplay Demo & 16K version' and a '48K version'. Spectrum Computing genre: Arcade Game: Action.

title: Pesky Painter
mechanics: Amidar-model grid capture: trace the edges of a fixed rectangular lattice, and a cell fills once its whole perimeter is traced (inferred from the GameBase 64 genre 'Arcade - Amidar'; no gameplay text found)
notes: GameBase 64 credits John Twiddy as programmer and comments 'a.k.a. "Amigo Painter"'.

title: Qiks
notes: A close arcade-accurate clone: you paint in the screen by drawing lines while avoiding the QIKS, a bouncing multicoloured line, plus other creatures that attack if you stay in one place too long, which matches Qix's Sparx/Fuse pressure. L. Curtis Boyle calls it the closest CoCo version to the arcade, closer than Tom Mix's Quix. Speech-cartridge support could not be verified and has been removed.

title: Qixi
mechanics: player marker moves along the border of a walled rectangular playfield (seen on the bottom edge in the in-game screenshot)
player draws a dotted trail from the border into the open field (Qix-style stix)
Qix-like enemy made of bouncing coloured line segments roams the open field
Sparx-like creature patrols the border near the player
controls: cursor keys plus space bar or Z, apparently Qix's draw buttons
notes: The title screen reads 'Qixi', 'by AS', 'Made 1984 by BBG-Software, Schimmelmannstr. 90, D-2070 Ahrensburg, West-Germany' and 'USE CURSOR KEYS AND SPACE BAR OR Z'. SharpMZ lists it as QUIXI: a machine-code (OBJ) program in English, 8 KB zipped, with the tape file QUIXI.mzf. The in-game screenshot shows a Qix layout: a bordered field, a player on the edge with a dotted trail rising into the field, a bouncing multi-line enemy and a border crawler. The screenshot shows no filled area, so area capture and the percentage target are inferred from the Qix lineage, not seen. The binary holds no gameplay text, such as score or percentage labels, that would confirm the rules.

title: Quix (CoCo)
developer: Claude R. Gagnon (original prototype by Steve Ostrom)
notes: A straight clone: you fill in the screen by drawing lines while avoiding monsters and the Quix, a travelling line. It is described as a little less arcade-faithful than Spectral's Qiks.

title: Squares (BBC Micro, Your Computer type-in)
publisher: Your Computer (IPC Electrical-Electronic Press Ltd.), magazine type-in, vol. 4 issue 4, April 1984
mechanics: Amidar-genre grid capture (bbcmicro.co.uk secondary genre 'Amidar'; no gameplay description found)
notes: The game's title is simply 'Squares'; the parenthetical tells it apart from the unrelated 1985 Spectrum type-in of the same name. Genre Maze, secondary genre Amidar.

title: Statix
mechanics: areas drawn at slow speed score triple points (Qix gives double)
notes: A straight Qix clone. The in-game instructions, copied from the tape inlay, describe the Statix charge (the Qix), sparks that follow you along the boundary (Sparx), fuses that run up your trail if you hesitate (Fuse), a 75% target with a bonus for each percent above it, and a faster, more aggressive Statix on each new screen. Its own copyright line reads 'COPYRIGHT PSION 1984'.

title: Xonix
developer: Dani Katz and Ilan Rav (spelled 'Ilan Raab' in English Wikipedia)
mechanics: the grid is split into claimed 'land' and open 'sea'; the cursor moves freely on land and leaves a trail only in the sea
sea balls move diagonally and bounce off land and off each other; a ball touching the trail costs a life
land enemies (a square 'spider') roam the claimed land, so the player is not safe there either
returning to land turns the trail into land and fills every sea pocket that holds no ball; pockets with a ball stay sea, and only the trail is converted
a set land percentage clears the level (75% per old-games.ru; Hebrew Wikipedia says the required share rises by level)
each new level adds one more ball, and balls get faster
notes: Founder of the Xonix family. Written by two Israeli soldiers during IDF service. Very popular in Israel and the USSR/CIS, including at the Dorodnicyn Computing Centre, and the template for most Soviet and Russian clones. A 2023 mirror of English Wikipedia says it was first written for the Electronika 60, which conflicts with the Hebrew account. The English Wikipedia article currently returns 404.

title: Antix
developer: Dmitry Pavlovsky (English Wikipedia adds Vadim Gerasimov; Hebrew Wikipedia credits Alexey Pajitnov)
mechanics: inverted Xonix: the field starts filled, and the goal is to clear a set percentage of it
balls bounce through the field and cost a life if they hit the player's line or the player
diamond-shaped enemies move hidden beneath the still-filled surface, invisible until they emerge, and kill on contact
level 1 starts with two balls and one diamond, and another diamond spawns after a while, which punishes stalling
later levels add enemies (MobyGames: one more ball per level), and ball speed rises over time
speed 1-9 chosen before play; the HUD shows score, percent cleared, lives and enemy count; high-score table
notes: Soviet game written first for the Elektronika 60 and then ported to DOS (CGA). Sources disagree on starting lives (5 per MobyGames/archive.org, 3 per old-games.ru) and on authorship.

title: Aree
publisher: Pubblirome (Super Game 2000 no. 3, April 1985; also on Top 30 no. 2 and Top 100 no. 1)
notes: An Italian budget-tape rebadge of Andrew Trott's Stix (Supersoft, 1983), which GameBase64 lists under Arcade - Qix. GB64 links the two entries and credits Trott as Aree's programmer and graphic artist. No changes to the gameplay are documented.

title: Blade Runner (C64, WizardSoft)
mechanics: Time Runner's grid capture, claiming boxes by tracing their edges; it is listed as a clone of Time Runner
notes: Unrelated to the film licence games. GameBase 64 lists it as a 'Clone Of' Time Runner, with the same programmers as Funsoft's C64 Time Runner, so it is most likely a retitled re-release. It is effectively a duplicate of the Time Runner entry. Wikipedia's maze list gives 1982, but the GameBase 64 entry it cites says 1985.

title: Hefro-Karo
publisher: Happy Computer (German magazine type-in, issue #20, June 1985, p. 83)
mechanics: Amidar-inspired grid capture (Spectrum Computing lists Amidar as its inspiration; no gameplay description found)
notes: German-language, single player. Spectrum Computing genre: Arcade Game: Action.

title: Qix (ZX Spectrum, PCW type-in)
publisher: Personal Computer World (type-in, February 1985 issue, p. 250)
mechanics: the Qix is a five-segment line that wanders at random early on but homes in on the player while drawing, more often as claimed area grows, and always from screen 4 onwards
one life is restored after each cleared screen, up to a maximum of 3
notes: Otherwise standard: two border patrollers start in the right-hand corners, and being caught sends you back to where the line started and costs a life. The listing's REM header says 1984, and ZXDB notes the printed program contained errors. The mechanics come from the archived BASIC listing.

title: Squares (Computronic type-in)
publisher: Computronic (German magazine type-in, Nov 1985 special issue '11 & 12')
mechanics: Amidar-inspired grid capture (Spectrum Computing lists Amidar as its inspiration; no gameplay description found)
notes: Freeware type-in in BASIC plus machine code. Single player; cursor keys or Kempston joystick. A Zuheir Urwani is also credited, with Thomas H. Kolbe, on the C64 Amidar clone Omidar (1987), which suggests the same author.

title: Territoire
mechanics: two snakes each mark out their own terrain; whoever encloses the most area wins
notes: Logic-and-action game, one of three on a Logimicro cassette with Avis de Recherche and Othello. Authors unknown per DCMOTO. An early competitive trail-territory game that predates .io games by about 30 years; lineage io-territory is a mechanic-family label, not descent. It is not stated whether the second snake is human or computer.

title: Kix (BBC Micro)
mechanics: 20 quadrants (scenes), each needing 75% coverage
in two-Sparkler scenes, a line that separates the Sparklers wins the quadrant at once and earns a split bonus (100 quick or 1000 slow)
each screen has a time limit shown as a bar, and the time left is paid out as a bonus
slow drawing is worth 10x quick drawing (30 vs 3 points per percent)
up to four Tracers patrol the lines, and some scenes have two fast-moving Sparklers
notes: Sparklers are Qix-like enemies, Tracers are Sparx and there is a Fuse if you hesitate. Hold the draw key for slow drawing; release it after starting for quick drawing. Extra life every 10,000 points. The mechanics come from the inlay instructions and the in-game text on the archived disc.

title: Panel Panic
mechanics: grid capture (listed by Wikipedia under Amidar-style 'grid capture games'; no gameplay description found)
notes: MSX Games World: tape, PSG sound, keyboard or joystick, single player, genre Action, also known as 'Panel Panique'. The gamecard URL that Wikipedia cites returns 404; the live page is software.php?id=1273.

title: Squixx
notes: A German PD title listed in Atarimania's Arcade - Qix genre. It is 1-player, uses a joystick and needs 0.5 MB and TOS 1.0. No description of its gameplay is available.

title: Torch 2081
mechanics: a fuel gauge limits flight time, and leftover fuel turns into points at the end of the level
you cannot travel along edges shared by two built panels, only along the outer perimeter and panel edges that face open space
stopping while building a panel makes the construction line unstable and destroys the glider (this replaces Qix's Fuse)
the Fireball (the Qix) changes speed and course to evade you
the Fireball releases Spitfires that fly straight at you and become more dangerous in later levels
every fifth level is a bonus level with two identical Fireballs: separating them raises the bonus multiplier, while capturing both gives a bonus glider and points but no multiplier
the starting difficulty rank is chosen on the title screen
notes: Crystal perimeter patrollers (Sparx), the coverage bonus above the required percentage and an extra glider every 10,000 points are also in the manual but are base Qix, so I dropped them from the mechanics. Wikipedia dates the game 1986, while the formatted manual carries a 1988 copyright, so the first-release year is uncertain.

title: Omidar
developer: Profiteam (programmers Thomas H. Kolbe and Zuheir Urwani)
publisher: Markt & Technik (Happy Computer magazine type-in, issue 1987/12)
mechanics: Amidar-model grid capture: trace the edges of a fixed rectangular lattice, and a cell fills once its whole perimeter is traced (Wikipedia lists it as an Amidar clone; GameBase 64 genre 'Arcade - Amidar')
notes: A magazine type-in, not a boxed release. Printed in Happy Computer 1987/12, then reprinted in 64'er Sonderheft 37 and 64'er Spielesammlung #4. Co-programmer Zuheir Urwani shares his name with the author of the 1985 Spectrum Amidar type-in Squares (Computronic).

title: Qix (Tilt type-in)
developer: M. V. Elias, refined by Erick Caberia
publisher: Tilt magazine (France), issue 3, March 1987 listings special '240 pages de listings', p. 188
mechanics: there is no line drawing: one key per side pushes each of the four playfield walls inward 2 pixels, scoring 1 point per push
a bouncing 'crazy line' (ligne folle) moves inside the box, and if it touches the wall you last moved you lose 0-19 points at random; there are no lives
a level is cleared at 150 points, and the line speeds up each level
notes: A minimal shrink-the-arena take on Qix rather than a real clone. The REM header names it 'FOOL-LINE' and says it was written by M. V. Elias and polished by Erick Caberia. The mechanics come from the archived BASIC listing.

title: Xonix (A. Surna)
notes: Lithuanian-language freeware. The database has no gameplay description and lists it as inspired by Qix; treated as a straight clone.

title: Xonix (Radio-86RK / Mikrosha)
notes: Russian Wikipedia lists Xonix among the most popular machine-code games for the Radio-86RK, a DIY design published in Radio magazine in 1986. It also lists 'Ксоникс' on the program cassettes shipped with the Mikrosha, a factory-built Radio-86RK clone in serial production from 1987. MAME has XONIX dumps for both machines (radio86_cass 'xonix', mikrosha_cass 'xonix'), and its Radio-86RK list also holds the variants XONIX-S, XONIX1 and XONIXZM. The year is estimated from the machines' dates. No gameplay description was found, so it is a straight clone as far as documented.

title: Zolyx
developer: Zoltán Tass (design and C64/C16 code; Plus/4 page also credits Gábor K. Kádas); ZX Spectrum version by Pete Cooke; CPC conversion by Lynsoft UK (B.J. Polausca)
mechanics: no Qix: several balls bounce inside the unclaimed area, and a ball touching the cursor or an unfinished line costs a life
enemy dots also roam the claimed area and kill on contact (Pelit: 2 in the open area and 2 in the claimed area at the start; Sinclair User: a larger blob chases you round the perimeter)
touching your own unfinished trail is fatal
at least 75% must be filled within a time limit, with bonus points for every percent above 75%
one extra ball is added each level
ZX Spectrum only: if an open line is kept going too long, a chaser ball comes up behind the cursor, capping line length
a limited stock of 'reverses' (a Plus/4 trainer offers unlimited reverses; the effect is undocumented)
notes: Budget £1.99. The Plus/4 version was Firebird's last C16 release. GB64 and ZXDB file it as a Qix clone, but play is Xonix-style: a safe claimed area, balls in the open area and dots roaming the claimed area. Crash's Kati Hamza says the killer ball was 'introduced specifically for the Spectrum' and makes 'long sweeping strokes across the screen impossible'; Crash panned the Spectrum port, while Sinclair User gave it 8/10.

title: Maniax
developer: Marc Ebner, with graphics by Wagner Bros (Atari ST); Jörg Dierks (C64, Plus/4)
publisher: Kingsoft; Anco Software (European Atari ST release)
mechanics: fenced-off areas reveal parts of photographs of cities around the world
letters fly around the field, and catching them (through a 'W' bonus tile) is meant to spell out the pictured location; this feature was left unfinished on Plus/4
death's-head and flame hazards (Plus/4)
two-player mode (C64)
notes: The Plus/4 release is buggy: the main enemy can freeze with completed areas left unpainted, so the level cannot be won, and the screen between levels flashes by in under a frame. The ST version was also released as a Floppyshop PD disk.

title: Power Styx
mechanics: closing shapes with the energy trail uncovers a hidden picture; 15 levels with a 75% target
monsters roam both the uncovered and the unrevealed areas
bonus symbols appear in newly uncovered space and give an extra life, more time, points or speed, or instant death
letters collected along the bottom of the screen win the level outright once they spell the full word
notes: Dazeland describes it as a Qix clone in which you rebuild an image frame by frame while avoiding the enemies. The more detailed rules come from the LaunchBox Games Database, which users edit.

title: Shocker
mechanics: the player moves only around the edge of the tank, using two switches (left and right)
the fire button sends a straight line across the tank to bisect it (the screenshot shows the line part-way across)
after a cut, every eel left in the smaller half is deactivated, scoring 100 points each, so the game discards the smaller part instead of the part without the enemy
electric eels swim in the open water and their bite is lethal
an optional 'blue reptile' creeps along the water's edge, like Sparx (switched on or off in the options)
per-player settings for game speed (fast, medium or slow) and how fast the eel moves compared with the man (same or faster)
1 player, or 2 players with the same or different settings
three-input accessible controls: Space, Z and X keys, or switches wired to the user port or the analogue port
notes: One of four games on Brilliant Computing's 'Arcade Adventure' compilation (Brickout, War Of The Worlds, Toboggan Run, Shocker), made to help disabled children play. The mechanics come from the instruction text in the program on the archived disc image and from the archive's screenshot. bbcmicro.co.uk lists it as single-player, but the program asks for 1 or 2 players.

title: Skyx
developer: Legend Software (code Alain Dubois, Eric Jourdan; graphics Alain Dubois, Didier Quentin; scenario Olivier Moraze)
mechanics: Zolyx-style capture combined with a Gauntlet-inspired adventure mode
choose one of four characters with their own traits (warrior, mage, elf, acrobat): the elf is very fast and the mage has a protective shield
a spark chases you as soon as you start drawing and catches you if the area you draw is too large
a green alien (or mask) moves fast across the screen and kills instantly if it touches the line you are drawing
other enemies travel along the lines you have already drawn
a witch works to limit your territory
pickups: apples regenerate you or give more time, 'Flums' give an extra life, and harmful 'Gnaps' potion bottles make you behave strangely, so not every pickup should be taken
20 different screens
notes: French release, created December 1988. Reviewers found it frustrating because of the fast green enemy, but it is an early example of character classes and pickups in a capture game.

title: Striker (MicroHobby type-in)
publisher: MicroHobby (Spanish magazine type-in, issue #166, March 1988); reissued on the compilation Spectrum Collection 1 (Ignacio Prini Garcia, 1989)
mechanics: Amidar-inspired grid capture (Spectrum Computing lists Amidar as its inspiration; no gameplay description found)
two players taking turns
notes: Spanish-language. Spectrum Computing genre: Arcade Game: Action.

title: Trix
mechanics: the required fill level (60% at first) rises as the game goes on, and points are scored for filling beyond it
notes: Otherwise a straight Qix clone. Edge patrollers that also run along your completed lines are Sparx, an enemy that chases you along the line you are drawing is the Fuse, and the large pulsating line enemy in the centre is the Qix. It starts straight into play with no title screen and needs Kickstart 1.3: under Kickstart 2 or 3 the player dies constantly. The 1988 date comes only from Wikipedia's clone list.

title: Zoom!
platforms: Sega Genesis / Mega Drive (1990, published by Sega)
mechanics: edge painting instead of area cutting: skate along the gridlines of 36 faux-3D isometric boards; each skated line changes colour, and a tile flashes once all its edges are coloured
clear condition is 100%: a board ends only when every line has been skated
Spiler enemies erase lines the player has already coloured, undoing progress
some enemy contacts slow the player instead of costing a life (Space Phantoms, Rowdy Fingers)
limited ammunition: a supply of rubber balls to shoot enemies
pickups: hourglass freezes all enemies, sun gives temporary invincibility, bananas slow some enemies, ribbon candy gives points
completing a board kills all its enemies
two players at once
notes: Amidar-style edge painting on an isometric grid, where an enemy can undo the player's painted edges. Wikipedia categorises it as developed in Germany. GameBase 64 credits Andy Hook as the C64 programmer. Genesis release: January 1990 in North America and Japan. That port got poor reviews (EGM average 3/10, MegaTech 45%).

title: Alien Blockade
mechanics: enclosed areas reveal part of a background picture
the background pictures are external Degas or Neochrome files, so players can swap in their own; the number of pictures is limited only by memory and disk space
'tracers' that move along the border are added on later levels
a countdown timer runs, and letting it run out costs a life
one large area scores more than several small ones
bonus for enclosing the alien energy field or a tracer
time bonus at the end of each level; an extra life every 10,000 points
notes: Version 1.0 is dated 1989 and version 1.1 1991. It is written in 68000 assembly and is joystick-controlled. An alien energy field roams the unfilled area and kills on contact with the cursor or with a line being drawn.

title: Bally III
notes: The Aminet readme describes it only as an 'Amiga port of the former arcade game named Click' and says this version is faster and fixes bugs. An earlier 'Bally' by the same author ('The First Version Ever anno 1988-89') is also on Aminet. The claim that it plays like Qix rests on a Lemon Amiga comment (the page returned 403 to me) and on the later Bally Five, which uses the same 'Bally' file names and is described as 'Quix like'. Its gameplay is not documented.

title: Electro Bingo
publisher: Sinclair User (covertapes: issue 87 Megatape 16, June 1989; issue 88 Megatape 17, July 1989; issue 89 Megatape 18)
mechanics: maze painting in the Make Trax model (Spectrum Computing lists Make Trax as its inspiration; no gameplay description found)
notes: Sinclair User cover-competition game in three parts. ZXSR notes it was 'not for general release'. Single player. Parts 2 and 3 are separate covertape entries rather than true alternate titles. No credited authors.

title: Graffity
mechanics: Amidar-style grid capture: surround every square with paint to clear the board
cleaner enemies wipe paint off already-painted edges, undoing the player's progress
notes: Spectrum Computing remarks: 'Action game in the vein of Zolyx or Quicksilva's Damper. Surround all squares with paint before the cleaners wipe it off.' Tagged as inspired by Make Trax. Dutch/English, single player.

title: Illgen
developer: Sebastian Broghammer (Byteriders); graphics Phillip Bergmann & D. Oppelt; music Stefan Hartwig
mechanics: two players claim territory at the same time on one field, each with their own score, lives and 'power' bar
the HUD shows a 'time pointer' bar beside a 'screen filled' bar
notes: CSDb lists a 1989 Byteriders release. It was published on the 64'er disk 1990/01 and again in 64'er 1999/07. A 1989 demo contains only level 2. The in-game screenshot shows sprites that look like planets and spaceships, and a per-player 'Snits' counter starting at 50 whose meaning is undocumented. It shows no picture reveal, so I removed the earlier claim about filling in a picture.

title: FANCY QIX
mechanics: claimed sections reveal a hidden background picture
the marker has a strength meter: each enemy collision drains it instead of costing a life outright, and the marker is destroyed when it runs out
barriers block some areas, so Stix cannot be drawn through them
target percentage to clear, with score added for every percent beyond it
notes: Unlicensed doujin release for the X68000, 1 player. LaunchBox lists it as homebrew. The research claim that it was the first to pair Qix capture with adult image reveal, a year before Gals Panic, could not be checked: dic.pixiv.net returned 403, and the LaunchBox page does not describe the picture as adult.

title: Tokimeki Cherry Box
alt_titles: ときめきチェリーボックス
notes: Japanese Wikipedia has only a one-line mention: a 陣取りゲーム (territory game) that reuses the setting of the Tokimeki Sports Gal series (1988) and led to 妖獣倶楽部 (Yōjū Club, also listed under 1990). D.O. is an adult-game maker, so the game is probably an adult image-reveal game, but neither its reveal mechanic nor its platform is documented.

title: XONIX (Spektr-001)
notes: Russian Wikipedia lists XONIX among the machine-code games on the cassette bundled with the Spektr-001, a Radio-86RK clone built by the Oryol UVM plant in the early 1990s and sold for 457 rubles in 1990. The Spektr-001 runs Radio-86RK software, so this is probably the Radio-86RK XONIX (entry 285), not a separate program. The Wikipedia article is tagged for deletion. Straight clone as far as documented.

title: Strong Lines
mechanics: claimed areas reveal a digitised photograph (animals such as a monkey and a rabbit)
the difficulty setting is the fill target to clear a level: 75%, 80%, 85% or 90%
a countdown timer runs in the HUD next to the fill %, score, lives and level
notes: German magazine coverdisk (ST Deluxe 1991/12) for 1 player with a joystick. Its options also include music on/off and 50/60 Hz.

title: Xonix (C&C)
notes: Russian-language TR-DOS freeware. No gameplay description in the database; straight clone as far as documented.

title: Bally Five
notes: Aminet calls it a 'Quix like action game'. The archive's files are dated 02-Sep-92 and 31-Dec-93, and it was uploaded in 1995. The executable and docs are named 'Bally', which matches Oliver Wagner's Bally (1988-89) and Bally III (1989), both 'Amiga port of the former arcade game named Click', but no author is stated. Its gameplay is not documented.

title: Smiley
mechanics: an options menu sets the number of players, 'Smileys' (probably lives), monsters, speed, and the starting fill target (65% shown)
a 'random pictures' option shuffles the order of the level pictures; the HUD counts pictures ('Bild 1/…')
notes: Version 1.6 is dated 15.04.1992 and written in GFA BASIC 3.5. The title screen says IDL Software GmbH, Darmstadt, holds exclusive usage rights and that paid redistribution is not allowed (licenceware). The text is in German. The options also include a 'Dynamik' on/off switch whose effect is undocumented.

title: Mega Xonix
notes: Russian-language TR-DOS freeware. No gameplay description in the database; treated as a straight clone.

title: Robo Xonix
notes: English-language TR-DOS freeware, later also distributed as a tape image (Scene+ 037). No gameplay description in the database; treated as a straight clone.

title: Xonix (Vlad Corp)
notes: English-language TR-DOS freeware. No gameplay description in the database; straight clone as far as documented.

title: Kwiks
mechanics: claimed areas reveal a true-colour photograph (e.g. a desert landscape); the HUD shows level, fill %, lives and points
up to four players, chosen with F1-F4 on the title screen (turn order not described)
notes: Public domain, made in Germany, needs about 2 MB of free RAM, runs in True Color VGA. The disk release has six level pictures, cut down to fit a 720 KB disk, and the author asks for new graphics and mods.

title: Kumquat
publisher: self-published shareware (demo on an Amiga Format coverdisk)
mechanics: clone of the C64 game Zolyx: fill a set amount of the screen without being hit by any of the enemy dots
notes: The shareware demo has 5 levels and was on an Amiga Format coverdisk in summer 1996. The author later released the full version for free, with its AMOS source on Aminet. Zolyx is often grouped with the Xonix-style bouncing-ball games, but I could not confirm how Kumquat's dots move.

title: AQuix
mechanics: the player dot moves freely on the frame and on claimed area; when it leaves, it turns into a 'Quix' that draws a trail
red star-shaped enemy Quixes bounce in the open area and destroy the player or trail on contact (one life); one more each level
pressing SPACE reverses every enemy Quix's direction, the player's only defence
only regions with no enemy Quix are filled; separating two enemy Quixes with one cut gives a 500-point bonus
points by the size of each area cut off; extra points and an extra life for finishing a level with more than 75% filled
a level is complete at 75%
runs in a MUI window on any public screen; the real-time high-score list scrolls the current position upward as the score rises
game state can be saved and loaded; colours of game elements are configurable
notes: Version 1.04 is dated February 26, 1997 and was uploaded to Aminet on January 23, 1998; earlier versions are undated. The German docs call it a 'Quix-Variante', but the rules are Xonix-like: free movement on claimed land, several bouncing enemies, and only enemy-free regions filled. The readme's blurb about balls and 'separating blocks' reads like JezzBall, but the game is not.

title: Lady in Love
developer: Bolivar di Griz and dr. Stanley
notes: ZXDB marks it 'Never released (demo available)', freeware, Arcade Game: Action, 1 player, and lists Taito's Volfied as its inspiration. No gameplay description or screenshot exists, so the mechanics are undocumented. The '[CENSORED]' title suffix suggests adult content, but the page shows no explicit x-rated flag.

title: 3Quarter
notes: A straight Qix clone: enclose 75% of the screen while avoiding a monster in the open field and sparks that travel along the borders and drawn lines. The packaging says '3Quarter' and the title screen '3Qurter'.

title: Atock
notes: Listed under GB64's Arcade-Qix genre as part of Multisoft's 'Arcadepack', 1 player, with documentation that is not online. The GB64 in-game screenshot shows drawn lines that run diagonally as well as orthogonally, forming box shapes, with insect-like enemies and a diamond-shaped cursor. Its rules are undocumented, so I did not list diagonal drawing as a mechanic.

title: Colour Qix
notes: Known only from the MAME Colour Genie cassette software list (entry 'colqix', year '198?', loaded with SYSTEM then QIX). The title suggests a straight Qix clone; its gameplay is not documented.

title: Ksoniks
notes: In MAME's Partner 01.01 cassette list the set 'xonix' has the description 'Ksoniks'. Its 1995-byte file has the same CRC32 (8da8f0d0) and SHA-1 as the Radio-86RK XONIX dump (radio86_cass 'xonix'), so it is the same program, not a separate port. Treat it as a near-duplicate of entry 285.

title: Qix (KC 85/2-4)
notes: The only evidence is that German Wikipedia's Qix article lists 'KC 85' among the ports, linked to Kleincomputer KC 85/2-4. It gives no author, year or description and is probably an unofficial clone. The KC 85/2-4 article itself does not mention Qix. Its gameplay is not documented.

title: Xonix (Elektronika BK-0010)
notes: MAME's BK-0010 cassette list has two separate programs, XONIX1 and XONIX5. Both are listed with year 19?? and an unknown publisher, and both are loaded from the Monitor. Gameplay is undescribed. Presumably straight Xonix clones.

title: Xonix (Lviv PK-01)
notes: Known only from MAME's Lviv cassette list: set 'xonix', a 1815-byte .lvt file loaded with BLOAD"",R, with year 19?? and an unknown publisher.

title: Xonix (Micron)
notes: MAME's Mikrosha cassette list has set 'xonmicr' (2822 bytes), titled 'Xonix (Micron)' and credited to Micron. It is distinct from the unattributed XONIX and XONIXZM in the same list. The name Micron also appears on a BASIC ('Бейсик «Микрон»') on the Spektr-001 bundled cassette and on an 'Assembler and Editor Micron' in MAME's Partner list. This suggests Micron was a Radio-86RK-family software label.

title: XONIX (Robotron 1715)
platforms: Robotron 1715 (East Germany, CP/M-compatible SCP; 1715M in the USSR)
notes: Known only from a screenshot. The Wikimedia Commons file Xonix.gif, uploaded in 2013 by Ris2002, is captioned 'Скриншот игры XONIX Robotron 1715' and sits in the category Games of the Soviet Union. The Robotron 1715 has only text modes (64x16 and 80x24), so this version must use text characters. Straight clone as far as documented.

title: Xonix (Specialist)
notes: Known only from MAME's Specialist cassette list: set 'xonix', a 2634-byte .rks file with year 19?? and an unknown publisher.

title: XONIXZM
notes: MAME has XONIXZM dumps for three Radio-86RK-family machines: Apogee BK-01 (3937 bytes), Radio-86RK (3832 bytes) and Mikrosha (3814 bytes). These look like per-machine ports of one program. It is distinct from the plain XONIX, XONIX-S and XONIX1 in the same Radio-86RK list, but may overlap with entry 285. Gameplay is undescribed.

title: JezzBall Beta 1 (TI-92, Chris Scott)
notes: Early calculator JezzBall (file dated 27 Apr 1997), known only from its ticalc.org listing: no description, documentation or source, about 5,271 downloads. Its mechanics cannot be checked.

title: JezzBall (TI-83, Joe Wingbermuehle)
mechanics: one more ball added each level
selectable ball speed setting (3 is the slowest)
score rewards dividing the room quickly
notes: v1.2 is dated 26 Aug 1998 and v2.0 (Ion, includes .8xp for TI-83 Plus) 25 Aug 1999. v2.0 ranks #22 on ticalc.org's all-time top downloads, with about 188,700 downloads.

title: JezzBall (TI-85 ZShell) and its TI-86/TI-92 ports
developer: unknown (TI-85 original); Fargo II conversions by Source Guru
notes: Straight clones. ticalc.org archive dates: TI-85 ZShell JezzBall v2.1 on 1998-05-14; separate TI-92 JezzBall v1.6 (needs flib) on 1998-09-09; Jezzball 86, 'a port from the ZShell game', on 1999-05-03; TI-85 Jezzball 2.2 converted to Fargo II by Source Guru in Feb-Apr 2000 (three uploads).

title: JezzBall (TI-92 / TI-89, Thomas Fernique)
mechanics: up to 20 balls (v1.3)
level 1 starts with 2 balls and 2 lives; each level adds one ball and one life (v1.8)
notes: 68k-calculator JezzBall with source included. v1.3 (9 Mar 1998, 'now 20 balls'), v1.6 (9 Sep 1998, needs flib), v1.8 (2 Feb 2001, TI-89 kernel, 'for any ROM version'). The v1.8 archive contains only a .89z binary.

title: Jezzball 82 (TI-BASIC)
mechanics: written in TI-BASIC; no extra ball is added per level (the author invites others to add it)
notes: Minimal BASIC JezzBall, file dated 10 Nov 1999.

title: JezzBall 48 / JezzBall 49
notes: Straight clone with high scores, in English and French. hpcalc.org describes it as a clone of 'the famous TI89 game'. HP 49 version 1.02 is dated 17 Apr 2001; HP 48 version 1.01 is dated 18 May 2001 and is 1 KB bigger because it bundles the minifont.

title: Vix
notes: A vector-display Qix clone on a homebrew cartridge shared with Tsunami, a Tempest-style shooter. The cartridge also holds a Magic 8 Ball program, a 'Saw Gallery' demo and a hidden message, and came in a standard edition and a numbered Collector's Edition. Its gameplay is not described beyond being a Qix clone.

title: 4kQix
notes: A Qix conversion fitted into 4 KB for the 2004 Oric minigames compo, where it ranked 14th. It is a straight clone: draw boxes, avoid the Qix and Sparx, and claim 75% to advance. Distributed as a TAP tape image.

title: Jezzball - Classic
mechanics: three difficulty levels
notes: Straight clone in C (TIGCC, no kernel needed). High scores are kept in an external file so the game can be archived. v1.15 is dated 3 Jan 2004; no earlier version is listed in the folder.

title: Late
developer: Caleb More / ToAks (uploaded by Tony Aksnes)
mechanics: mouse-aimed cutter: left button fires, right button rotates it in 90-degree steps
a fired cut cannot be stopped; it runs until the cut completes or a ball strikes it
the cutter survives a few ball hits instead of dying on the first
goo balls split and scatter when hit, then can reform
unstable triples: groups of three balls that explode when enclosed tightly enough
teleporting balls jump to new positions
'cold-blooded' balls home in on the cutter when they see it
notes: Aminet short description: 'An Qix/Styx/Barrack clone'. Version 1.0, dated 2005-11-20, requires OS4 Pre 3 or later. Its enemy roster is unusually varied for the JezzBall family.

title: QiZX
notes: Spanish-language, one-player Qix-inspired game written in pure BASIC. It placed 2nd in the 'Pure BASIC' category of the Bytemaniacos Concurso BASIC 2007. Two TAP versions and an instructions file exist, but no gameplay description is published, so treat it as a straight clone.

title: JezzballDS
publisher: freeware homebrew (PAlib forum / Google Code rxitr-games)
mechanics: dedicated buttons for vertical (X) and horizontal (Y) walls in addition to the orientation toggle
level select of any level already reached (v1.3.0)
optional stylus 'stretch' mode for placing walls
speed and sound toggles in the options menu
notes: DS JezzBall clone built with PAlib, latest version 1.3.0 (2008-06-10); the initial release date was not found. raulbojalil's separate homebrew ports are related but not by this developer: 'Jezzball 3DS', based on JezzballDS (2015, adds stereoscopic 3D and SD-card high scores, with a Wii version added to the same repo), and JezzballU for Wii U (2016).

title: Xonix (TS-Config)
notes: Homebrew listed in MAME's tsconf software list as 'Xonix', year 2012, publisher <homebrew>, developer Shiru, file xnx.spg. MAME documents no gameplay.

title: Cix
mechanics: simultaneous two-player mode (the arcade Qix alternates players)
notes: One- or two-player Qix-inspired cartridge homebrew for the ColecoVision, released worldwide.

title: Jezzball v1.0 (TI-83 Plus / TI-84 Plus, Kerm Martian)
mechanics: clear threshold lowered to 65% per level
fill bonus proportional to how far past 65% you fill
time bonus for clearing a level quickly
notes: File dated 1 Dec 2013. The author says it follows the original PC rules with a few tweaks for calculators.

title: Clostro
mechanics: 8 fixed levels with an ending
separate keys for vertical (Q) and horizontal (E) walls instead of an orientation toggle
notes: JezzBall clone in Octo for Octojam 7 (October 2020), on a 64x32 playfield. A hidden cheat code exists. Source: clostro.8o on GitHub.

title: Atomix (BBC Micro)
notes: Written around 1990 and first released in 2021. bbcmicro.co.uk lists the primary genre as 'Avoid 'em' and the secondary genre as 'Qix'. It is one-player, keyboard only, runs on the Model B but not the Model A, and is untested on the Master. No gameplay description is published. Unrelated to Thalion's 1990 molecule puzzle game Atomix.

title: Amidar (Salvador Camacho)
notes: Homebrew maze game inspired by Konami's Amidar, written in compiled BASIC. Released 26 February 2022. Won 1st place in the Free/Compiled BASIC category of the Bytemaniacos Concurso BASIC 2022. Spanish-language. Spectrum Computing gives no gameplay description, so it is treated as a straight Amidar clone.

title: Mix
mechanics: a round timer: running out of time costs you the round, rather than releasing Super Sparx
constant line-drawing speed (no fast/slow draw)
cutting off a Tracer (border enemy) outside the play area scores bonus points, and it respawns after a short delay
in levels with several big green monsters, separating them with a line clears the level as if 100% were painted and doubles the time bonus
notes: MSXdev'22 entry #09, published 28 April 2022. Red Tracers patrol the edges, and a big green monster destroys unfinished lines. v1.1 and v1.2 (May 2022) fixed the time bonus and coverage computation and let the main enemies move diagonally. It is written for the TNIASM assembler, and the source is on GitHub.

title: Qyx
developer: Champ Games (John W. Champeau code/design; Nathan Strum art; Bob DeCrescenzo audio)
mechanics: simultaneous 2-player co-op modes via the QuadTari adapter (the arcade alternates players)
four skill levels (Novice, Standard, Advanced, Challenge); Challenge adds extra enemies
99 stages, each with a territory threshold; level bonus plus extra points for beating the goal
notes: Released October 2022. It keeps the arcade's core faithfully: the Fuse when you stall while drawing, Super Sparx on the stage timer that chase you onto the Stix, two Qyx in later stages with a multiplier for splitting them, fast and slow draw on 2-button pads, and the Spiral Death Trap. High scores save to AtariVox/SaveKey and feed the 'Qyx Kickers' list. Not compatible with the RetroN 77. Wikipedia lists it among Qix clones.

title: Amidoh!
notes: Released 23 September 2023 on itch.io. Spectrum Computing lists it as inspired by Konami's Amidar (genre 'Arcade Game: Action'), with redefinable keys and English text, but gives no gameplay description. Treated as an Amidar-style clone.

title: Kidelyneen
notes: A Qix-inspired one-player joystick game in Commodore BASIC V2. It must be compiled with the author's MOSpeed compiler to run at speed and is 'very very (very) slow' in the interpreter. A cracked release by Really Proud Lamers appeared on CSDB on 7 Sept 2023. No gameplay additions are documented, so treat it as a straight clone.

title: QIXSCII
mechanics: PETSCII character-cell playfield and trails
the area to fill is found by scanning the whole screen in compiled BASIC, so each capture takes noticeable time; a separate FASTFILL build swaps in a machine-code fill routine
notes: About 200 lines of BASIC V2 (excluding REMs), compiled with Blitz!, written for the Forum64.de 'Qix in BASIC V2' programming challenge. The original goal of 10 lines proved impossible. The BASIC listing is published as a PDF. The FASTFILL build was released 16 Sept 2023 after player requests. Otherwise a straight clone.

title: Xonix (Atari 8-bit)
mechanics: three threats: bouncing balls, 'shady characters' that follow the player, and the player's own trail
5 lives, with an extra life every 2 levels
game speed selectable from 3 to 9
two control modes: continuous movement, or move only while the stick is held
notes: Written in compiled Pascal, from Ukraine, distributed as an XEX file. The in-game credit reads '(C) by Andy Omelyanenko in 2024'. The title screen also has 'Original author:' and 'Ported to Atari:' lines, so it presents itself as a port of Xonix. The file in the Atarimania dump is dated 6 Mar 2024.

title: Painter Man!!
mechanics: paint every wall of a castle room to move on (maze-coverage goal, no enclosure); 10 levels
AI lions chase the player through the maze
a button spills paint on the floor; lions avoid the spill and turn away (placeable deterrent)
spills can be used to trap lions, for example inside the central 'O' shapes on level 2
notes: 128K and Enterprise versions released 1 May 2025, 48K version 3 May 2025. Made with MPAGD, with AY sound. The itch page pitches it to fans of Pac-Man and BurgerTime. The player is Banky Van Daime.

title: Qixie
mechanics: two Sparks patrol only the outer border in opposing patterns and never enter the field or follow drawn lines, making it easier than the arcade
the Qix moves in a sawtooth pattern, partly homes on the player, and makes sudden speed-ups and zoom-aways
notes: Written for the Commodore PET in 6502 machine language (C64 Studio) after attempts with the PetSpeed and RTL-BASIC compilers failed. Inspired by Roman Werner's QIXSCII. The author credits Claude with the Qix line-drawing and sawtooth/seeking movement code, and ChatGPT with help on trail logic. A C64 build with source code was released on CSDB on 16 May 2025. SNES-pad support was removed in a mid-May update. Capture uses a flood fill with PETSCII graphics. The author has floated A* pathfinding for Sparks in a future version.

title: Jeezball
mechanics: capture 75% of the screen with horizontal and vertical walls
a ball hitting a wall under construction removes the wall and costs a life
notes: Published on itch.io on 27 Oct 2026. Supports keyboard, mouse or two-button joystick and compensates for PAL/NTSC timing. Tested only in VICE. The page discloses AI-assisted code.

title: Jezzball NES
mechanics: walls grow in two halves (red up/left, blue down/right); a half that reaches solid ground turns to stone, a half touched by an atom is destroyed and costs a life
75% to advance; more atoms each level up to a cap of 12; levels cap at 99 then repeat
the play clock always runs
fully deterministic from power-on: the run-recap screen shows score, stats, RNG seed and an 8-hex CRC32 code binding the recap to one exact input sequence
verifier tool replays a submitted .fm2 input recording against the SHA-256-pinned ROM and prints per-level checkpoint codes
9-digit score that saturates instead of rolling over
notes: 'A fan tribute to JezzBall for the NES' in pure 6502 assembly at 60 fps, sharing no code or assets with the original. It ships a bot player, smoke tests and a 12-atom worst-case frame audit. Score submissions are an input recording plus a photo of the recap screen. Its replay-verifiable competitive design is directly comparable to Jiro-ikusu's journal verification. First commits are dated 18 July 2026.

title: Pauper.Io!
publisher: Freeware (Plus/4 World; part of the Proky Casual Collection)
mechanics: player against 3 bot opponents, each starting with a territory of at most 3x3 character cells
leave your territory, draw a trail and return to claim the enclosed area
an opponent cutting your unfinished trail eliminates you; crossing your own unfinished trail also ends the run
cutting an opponent's trail eliminates it and gives you its territory and its unfinished trail
walls do not kill: they stop movement or redirect it along the boundary
eliminated bots respawn at random free spots; you win when all three are out and no free space is left for them to return
score is your peak territory in cells, out of 3,588 playable cells
practice mode whose results do not count toward high scores
keyboard, joystick or mouse control (serial mouse over ACIA, or 1351 mouse via SID card); the mouse sets a direction and movement continues
notes: Released 2026-10-24. Plus/4 World files it under Game/Qix. 64K machine code, PAL only, marked AI assisted. Brings the Paper.io formula to an 8-bit machine.

title: PIX (Sega Genesis / Mega Drive)
mechanics: fully simultaneous local 2-player co-op (not alternating turns)
dedicated teleport button (B on pad, X on keyboard)
claimed area reveals hidden pixel-art pictures; completed pictures are saved to a gallery viewable from the title menu
a round clears either at the reveal percentage or by trapping every enemy inside claimed areas
five picture books: Scenes, Creatures, History, Mosaics (mathematically defined art) and Freestyle (pictures the players draw themselves)
notes: Version 0.1. The ROM is tested in RetroArch (Genesis Plus GX) and on flash carts. The itch.io page is dated Sept 2026 and was updated 5 Nov 2026. The listing is marked AI-assisted for code, graphics and text, and the developer says the artwork was generated with AI and then edited. The developer cites the 1981 Qix as inspiration; the picture-reveal mechanic is shared with the Gals Panic family.

title: QIXY
developer: Vattenmelon (Erling Reizer, with Claude AI credited)
notes: GB64 lists it as Arcade - Qix: one player, joystick port 2, with documentation and a loading screen. Erling Reizer and Claude AI are credited for code, music and graphics. A Blazon crack with 2 trainers exists. No gameplay description is available.

title: QL-x
notes: Published 30 Oct 2026 for the Retro Programmers United for Obscure Systems Sinclair QL jam, distributed as a microdrive image with a BOOT script. It is arcade-faithful: 75% target, bonus per percent above 75%, border-only movement unless Space is held to draw, safe from the creature on the border but Sparks on the border are lethal, three lives. The listing is marked AI-assisted (code): Claude helped optimise 68k graphics routines. Separate from Jgl's QLix.

title: QLix (Sinclair QL)
notes: Published 16 Oct 2026 as a microdrive image (QLix.mdv) for the Retro Programmers United for Obscure Systems Sinclair QL jam 2026. The page says only 'A Qix clone', so treat it as a straight clone. Separate from croguet's QL-x.

title: Gravity (GBA)
platforms: Game Boy Advance (ROM for flashcart or emulator)
publisher: VG Source Game Studio (self-published on itch.io, $3+)
mechanics: several enemy types with their own movement patterns instead of one Qix plus Sparx
new enemy types appear as the levels progress
an enemy touching the ship, or cutting the open line before it closes, costs a life
a level is cleared at a 'victory percentage' (most of the screen); the page does not give the threshold
notes: A paid homebrew ROM (GravityGBA.gba, 8 MB) built for real GBA hardware. The itch page never names Qix, but it describes the Qix loop: move along the safe edge, trace lines, and close them onto the edge or captured land. Its tags are Survival, Survivor-like and Space. The page shows no publish date, only 'Updated 08 Nov 2026'. Its itch game id (4063504) suggests the page was created around late 2025 or early 2026, which is an estimate only.

title: JayBall
platforms: Game Boy Advance (ROM, distributed for Windows/macOS via emulator)
mechanics: single bouncing ball; you win by trapping it in a region smaller than 625 pixels, not by reaching an area percentage
notes: JezzBall recreation made for a CS 2261 course assignment. It explores the GBA's Mode 3 bitmap mode. The itch.io page lists Windows and macOS as download platforms and recommends an emulator such as mGBA.

title: MOLTBALL C64
notes: Straight JezzBall-style wall-building containment clone, shipped as a single 14 kB moltball.prg. Framed as a compiled binary 'found' on a floppy labelled MOLTBALL, with no source. The itch.io AI disclosure lists AI assistance for code and graphics. Name-your-own-price.

title: Quark Panic
mechanics: cursor fires a gluon divider whose lines extend horizontally or vertically until they hit the screen edge or solid area
completed lines become solid, and any enclosed area with no quark also becomes solid
a quark hitting a line while it extends destroys the line and costs a life
stage clears at 75% solid (lower than JezzBall's 75-80% norm only in theme, not rule)
34 stages, each with more quarks
notes: JezzBall clone themed as a failed lab experiment releasing quarks. Written in C with the Wonderful Toolchain; music made in Furnace and played with the Cygnals library. Ships as .wsc (WonderSwan) and .fx (WonderWitch); tested in Mesen 2, Ares and on hardware with a FlashMasta flashcart. The itch.io page shows no publish date.

title: Territory Grid
mechanics: leave your safe zone, draw a wide path and reconnect it to your home area to claim new land
opponents can sever your path while it is exposed
the grid changes constantly during play
the player with the largest territory at the end wins
notes: Prototype. Described as a fast pixel-art territory battle game. The page does not name Paper.io or call itself a remake. The itch.io URL is under froggyvr2 while the listed author is m4v_dev, and the download files are named 'reddart'. The page says no generative AI was used.

title: Fortix
publisher: Nemesys Games (PC); VGChartz lists Complete-IT for the PSP minis release
mechanics: stage goal is to capture all of the enemy forts' area, not a screen percentage
towers guarding the forts shoot at the player once a line is started; a hit on the open line kills
capturing a crossed-swords trigger point fires a single-use catapult at a tower; the player cannot pick the target
a tower can be captured directly: bait it into wasting a shot, then loop round it while it reloads
anything enclosed by a capture (tower or dragon) dies permanently
three dragon types (fire-breathing, randomly flying, one that attacks once you start drawing); bats run along drawn lines like Sparx
capturing a key opens gates of the same colour; captures can trigger effects elsewhere on the map
rivers, mountains and cliffs slow movement and drawing; crossing a fort wall is very slow
walls block movement and cannot be used to close a line
randomly appearing power-ups
the line in progress can be retracted
drawing starts automatically on entering unclaimed land (no draw button)
a crown on the level map for a no-death clear, and optional time bonuses
notes: PSP minis: EU Oct 1, 2009, US Nov 23, 2009 (12 levels, per VGChartz's review). PC: Apr 12, 2010 (22 levels, per Gamepressure). VGChartz notes that claiming most of the screen usually also gives 'mission accomplished', but this is not required. Knight vs dragons fantasy theme.

title: Fortix 2
mechanics: 'reverse turret defence' framing: storm castles while dodging tower turrets and roaming monsters
maze-like level layouts
castle-to-castle campaign of 30 levels across 3 lands, ending against the mage Xitrof
Steam leaderboards
notes: Steam release May 6, 2011; Linux on Steam Sep 17, 2013. Indie Game Challenge finalist. A PS3 version could not be verified, and the official site fortix2.com is now an unrelated parked site.

title: Lightfish
publisher: Eclipse Games (self-published; Steam lists no publisher)
mechanics: goal is to destroy every monster in the zone by enclosing it, not to reach a percentage
enclosed enemies die but respawn after a delay, so speed matters
any enemy touching the fish itself kills it instantly
10 enemy types
lava squares act as walls and kill on touch
ice blocks (late game) slow the player but not the enemies
walls block movement and cannot be used to close a line; capturing them removes them
randomly appearing power-ups
the line in progress can be retracted
45 levels, 2 game modes and per-level score challenges
notes: Steam release Oct 19, 2011; full controller support, leaderboards. Neon sea-life outline art in a fast 'Qix as Robotron' style (wurb.com). The Mac and Xbox Live Indie Games versions could not be verified: Steam lists Windows only, and the developer site and Giant Bomb were blocked.

title: Space Xonix
mechanics: the player is a UFO claiming territory in space
a choice of upgrades is offered at each level
local co-op on one shared screen
online leaderboards and achievements
hazards include lasers, fireballs and lava (from a review quoted on the Steam page, not the official description)
notes: Released on Steam on 17 September 2015. Localized in English, French, German and Russian. The 'Space Zonix' spelling is a typo in a Ukrainian Wikipedia reference, not a real alternative title.

title: Cosmonix
mechanics: space setting: clear enclosed areas while avoiding enemies
enemies and obstacles include asteroids, mines and missiles
